articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

TL;DR: I keep seeing the same posts on most of the DEV home feed tabs: Discover, Following and Curated.

Wanted to fix it by implementing a simple Mark as Seen browser extension. Then one thing led to another, and I ended up building three projects: one already abandoned, and two ongoing (Feedgrab & Ghostify).

Note for users: This is still under development, so if you see errors, please look for updates: https://github.com/SweaDev/ghostify/releases

Note for judges: v1.0.0 was completed within the submission period; later releases are updates.

Backstory

These days, I spend too much time on DEV.

  • Deleted my old X/Twitter account because it gives me a headache! Created a new one only as a placeholder.
  • Deactivated my Facebook account, because it's… well, that's a story for another day!

So most of the time I spend online is here on DEV and YouTube.

But the problem with DEV (and YouTube too) is that I keep seeing the same posts in the feed!

Open DEV in the morning: there's that post. Open it at lunch: there it is again. Open it at night: guess who's back! I've read it. I've reacted to it. I may have even commented on it. Still there, staring at me like it hasn't been introduced yet.

So on October 26, I did what any sane developer would do: I opened my editor instead of closing the tab.

Attempt #1: myDEV (RIP 🪦)

The plan was simple:

  • Put a ✓ button on every post card, right next to Bookmark.
  • Click it, and the post disappears from the feed and goes into a new myDEV tab.
  • Done. Go back to reading.

And it worked! For about an hour. Then I opened YouTube and saw the same video for the 14th time this week, and realized myDEV only knew how to read one site, with selectors I hard-coded by hand. The moment DEV changes a class name, it's dead. And for YouTube, I'd have to start over.

It took me a few days to admit it, but today I finally archived it. Rest in peace, myDEV. You were too specific for this world.

Attempt #2: Feedgrab

What I actually needed wasn't a DEV plugin. I needed something that could look at any page and say: "this is a feed, these are the items, and this one is the same item you saw before, even after infinite scroll re-rendered it."

That became Feedgrab, a TypeScript library that:

  • detects feeds on a page (structural heuristics, optionally refined by an LLM), or takes CSS/XPath selectors you type;
  • lets you confirm or fix its guesses in a Shadow DOM overlay;
  • turns the feed into one de-duplicated stream of items that keeps up with infinite scroll;
  • never removes anything unless you ask it to.

It runs in browser extensions, headless browsers and on the server, with the same API.

Attempt #3: Ghostify

And then, finally, the thing I wanted in the first place. On top of Feedgrab. With a ghost. 👻

What I Built

Ghostify is a browser extension (Chrome + Firefox) for feeds that keep showing you the same posts.

Hover a post, click the ghost, and it's gone from the feed. For good. Reload, scroll, come back tomorrow: it stays gone.

But it's not deleted. It becomes a ghost. Ghostify keeps a copy, so you can find it again, read it later, or snooze it until the weekend.

That's my take on Ghost in the Machine: the posts you've already seen don't die, they just stop haunting your feed and move into the machine. Quietly. Politely. Until you call them back.

What it does:

  • The ghost button shows up on the post under your pointer. Click it, the post vanishes, and an Undo toast gives you 5 seconds of regret.
  • The Ghostify page keeps everything in three tabs: Ghosted, Later and Snoozed.
  • Snooze a post until later today, tomorrow, the weekend, next week, or any date. When time's up, it shows up in Back from snooze.
  • Search your ghosts by keyword, or switch on Semantic and just describe what you remember ("that post about JavaScript adding objects and arrays").
  • Auto-ghostify rules in plain English, per site: "recurring weekly discussion threads I have already read". A local decision model checks new feed items against them and ghosts the matches. If it gets one wrong, Not this brings the post back, and that rule never touches it again.
  • Add any site. On any page with a feed, click Add this site. Feedgrab proposes the feeds, you confirm them in its overlay, and choose whether they're for the logged-in or logged-out view.
  • New tab flavor, if you want your ghosts on every new tab.

Demo

No store listing (yet!), so the demo is: install it, open DEV, start ghosting. It takes about a minute:

  1. Download a zip from Releases: ghostify-<version>-chrome.zip or ghostify-<version>-firefox.zip.
  2. Chrome: unzip, open chrome://extensions, turn on Developer mode, click Load unpacked. Firefox: open about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox, click Load Temporary Add-on… and pick the zip.
  3. Open https://dev.to/ logged out, hover a post, click the ghost.

Here's a quick tour. (The screenshots represent what a user would see.)

The toolbar popup lists your recent ghosts. Click the 👁 to unghost one, and it shows up in the feed again:

Click a ghost to see its details, the AI summary and tags:

Write auto-ghostify rules in plain English, per site:

And pick a model for each job:

Code

SweaDev / ghostify

Ghostify Feed Browser Plugin (beta)

Ghostify

Ghostify is a browser extension (Chrome and Firefox) for feeds that keep showing you the same posts. Hover a post, click the ghost, and it disappears from the site's feed for good. Ghostify keeps a copy so you can find it again later.

v1.0.0. Ghostify works on the dev.to home feeds out of the box, and you can add any site. It has a full Ghostify page with snooze and search, and optional AI that runs locally with Ollama or with your own OpenRouter, Gemini or OpenAI key.

Features

  • The dev.to logged-out home feeds (Relevant /, Latest /latest, Top /top/*) are recognized automatically, through feedgrab.

  • The ghost button shows on the post under your pointer. Clicking it hides the post and saves it, and an Undo toast lets you take it back.

  • Ghosted posts stay hidden when you reload, and also when they come back…

View on GitHub

SweaDev / feedgrab

Feed Detector

Feedgrab

A TypeScript library that finds and describes content feeds in web pages (post timelines search results, product grids, article lists) and turns them into one de-duplicated stream of items with exclusion reports (ads, promoted posts, injected widgets).

  • Detect feeds automatically (structural heuristics, optionally refined by an LLM), by inspecting an element, or from CSS/XPath selectors you type.
  • Confirm/edit the proposals in a Shadow-DOM overlay, or programmatically with headless helpers.
  • Iterate a unified feed that keeps up with infinite scroll (MutationObserver) or pagination (ingest), with a report per item: kept, excluded (and why), or pending.
  • Exclude items by specificity-ranked selector rules, built-in ad rules, or plain-language LLM criteria. Nothing is removed unless you call a removal helper.

It runs in browser extensions (Chromium + Firefox, MV3), headless browsers (Playwright/Puppeteer injected bundle), and server-side (Bun/Node with a parsed DOM), using the same API everywhere.

Install

…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The open-source AI part

AI is optional and off by default. Ghostify is perfectly happy as a dumb "hide this post" button. Turn AI on, and it gets three jobs, each with its own model:

Job Default (local, via Ollama) Used for
Embeddings embeddinggemma-2 Semantic search over your ghosts
General gemma4:e2b Summaries and tags for each ghosted post
Decision d3:2b Checking new feed items against your auto-ghostify rules

All three are open-weight and small enough to run on a laptop. Start Ollama so it accepts requests from extensions, and that's it:

ollama pull embeddinggemma-2
ollama pull gemma4:e2b
ollama pull d3:2b
OLLAMA_ORIGINS="chrome-extension://*,moz-extension://*" ollama serve

If you'd rather use a hosted model, every job can switch to OpenRouter, Gemini or OpenAI with your own key. The plumbing is the AI SDK, so swapping providers is a dropdown, not a rewrite.

A few things I'm happy about:

  • Fallbacks everywhere. If the decision model is down, the general model handles the rule check. If embeddings fail, search falls back to keywords. Nothing breaks because Ollama isn't running.
  • Embeddings are tagged with the model that made them. Change the embedding model and Ghostify ignores the old vectors instead of mixing them up. Reindex fills the gaps.
  • One honest gap: d3's response format isn't documented (yet). Ghostify reads the shapes it knows, treats anything else as "no match", and logs it. Better to miss a ghost than to hide something you wanted to see!

The extension part

  • WXT for one codebase that builds Chrome MV3 and Firefox, plus the new-tab flavor.
  • React 19 + Tailwind v4 for the popup, the Ghostify page and settings.
  • Dexie (IndexedDB) for ghosts, embeddings and keys. Everything stays in your browser. No account, no sync, no server.
  • Feedgrab for finding feeds and items, and for hiding them. Ghostify never touches a feed node itself; it asks Feedgrab's removeItem to hide it, and its own UI lives in a separate Shadow DOM.

Security was a bit of a rabbit hole:

  • Content scripts never see API keys. They don't even open IndexedDB. Everything goes through typed messages to the background script, and the background talks to the model.
  • Keys aren't in storage.local either, because content scripts can read that. They live in a Dexie table on the extension's own origin.
  • In content scripts, Feedgrab gets a proxy instead of a model, which also shrank the bundle from 380 KB to 71 KB. Nice side effect!

The "how did you build all this in a week" part

I didn't write most of the code by hand. I used a coding agent.

But I didn't just say "build me an extension" either. I've been using a small spec-driven flow I call specx:

  1. Spec: I wrote the spec by hand. It's 17 lines. Literally a paragraph and a list of features.
  2. Plan: the agent turned it into a plan with the stack, architecture and a Decisions log.
  3. Tasks: then into 23 tasks across 4 phases, each with the spec/plan line ranges it needs, the files it touches, and a Done check.
  4. Build loop: take the first unblocked task, read only what it references, implement it, run its Done check plus lint + typecheck + tests, tick the box, commit. Repeat.
  5. Phase check: at the end of each phase, follow the README from a clean state, build, load it in the browser, fix what's broken, tag a release.

The rules live in AGENTS.md, so any agent can pick it up. Every judgment call goes into the plan's Decisions log, so I can see why something was done the way it was. And there's one commit per task, so git log reads like a changelog.

Phase 1 was "ghost a post on DEV". Phase 4 was "auto-ghostify with local AI". Each phase ended with something I could actually load and use, not a pile of half-wired modules.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because the thing Ghostify reads is my browsing.

Think about what an AI feature in a feed extension actually sees: every post on every feed you scroll, what you hide, what you save for later, what you search for. That's a pretty detailed picture of a person. I don't want that going to anyone's API by default. Not even mine.

With open-weight models, it doesn't have to:

  • Gemma 4 E2B, EmbeddingGemma 2 and d3:2b run on my laptop. Summaries, tags, semantic search and the rule checks all happen locally. With Ollama, nothing leaves the machine.
  • It costs nothing per post. Auto-ghostify checks every new item in the feed. With a paid API, that's a meter running every time I scroll. Locally, it's just my fan spinning a bit.
  • It keeps working. No rate limits, no deprecation emails, no "this model will be retired on…".
  • A small, specialized model is enough. I don't need a giant model to answer "is this a weekly discussion thread?" A 2B decision model is the right size for the job, and I could only pick it because it's open.

And it's not just the models. Ghostify is built on open source all the way down: WXT, React, Dexie, the AI SDK, Biome, Vitest… and Feedgrab, which I split out because I wanted it to be reusable. If someone wants to build a "hide the reruns" extension for YouTube, or a feed reader for a site that doesn't have RSS, the hard part is already there. MIT licensed. Go for it.

A closed API would have given me a smarter summary, maybe. Open models gave me a tool I'm actually comfortable running on everything I read.

My Agent Session

The whole project was built in agent sessions, following the specx flow above. The best way to see them is the commit history: one commit per task, from Scaffold WXT React project to Add auto-ghostify rules with rescue.

The Spirit of It

I keep thinking about the name.

Most "hide this" features are really "delete this". You click, it's gone, and you'll never find it again. That always felt a bit wrong to me. I did read that post. Some of them were good! I just don't need to see them every time I open the home page.

So in Ghostify, nothing dies. It becomes a ghost. It stays in the machine, with its title, its author, a little summary, and a few tags, waiting until you call it back. A bit like Día de los Muertos for posts: not here anymore, but not forgotten either.

And somewhere in an archived repo, myDEV is resting peacefully, knowing it started all of this. 🕯️

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Ghostify uses Gemma 4 E2B (gemma4:e2b) for summaries and tags, and EmbeddingGemma 2 (embeddinggemma-2) for semantic search, both running locally through Ollama by default.

Thanks for reading! And if a post of yours disappears from my feed, don't take it personally. It just means I've probably already read it, seen it, or will read it later. 👻

articles.title: I grepped for @ts-ignore and found zero. Then I grepped for the cast nobody bans
articles.description: Every TypeScript team has a rule about @ts-ignore. Ours does too, and it works: zero occurrences...
articles.body_html:
Every TypeScript team has a rule about @ts-ignore. Ours does too, and it works: zero occurrences across 610 source files.

Then I grepped for something nobody puts in a style guide:

grep -rn --include='*.ts' --include='*.tsx' \
  --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.next \
  'as unknown as' apps packages | wc -l

117.

Zero explicit suppressions, a hundred and seventeen implicit ones. That ratio is not a coincidence — it is what a ban creates when the ban only covers the syntax people remember to grep for.

The numbers, from a real repo

Pattern Occurrences in source
@ts-ignore 0
@ts-expect-error 0
as any 3
as unknown as 117
eslint-disable* 53
console.log 4

Two more facts worth having. The 53 eslint-disables are not 53 decisions: 42 of them are one rule (@next/next/no-img-element), which is a single architectural choice about <img> tags, repeated. And the casts are not evenly spread — they cluster:

File as unknown as
api/src/routes/admin.ts 14
api/src/stories/worker.ts 11
api/src/app.ts 7
api/src/assistant/worker.ts 6
web/src/lib/messages/index.ts 5
api/src/stories/production.ts 5

That distribution tells you what the casts are for. Admin routes parse request payloads. Workers deserialise rows that came back from the database as unknown. The i18n map indexes strings by a computed key. These are all boundaries — the places where a runtime shape meets a compile-time type and nobody wrote the parser.

Why this one survives code review

as unknown as Foo is two casts. The first erases the type to unknown, which is honest; the second asserts it back to whatever you want, which is the lie. Together they are semantically identical to as any, with three advantages:

  1. It compiles under no-explicit-any. If your lint config bans any — most do — this is the way around it.
  2. It reads as deliberate. A reviewer skimming a diff sees a cast, not a suppression comment. There is no red flag to grep for in review.
  3. It is what an agent reaches for. When a model is asked to make a type error go away, as unknown as is the minimal edit that satisfies the compiler without adding a comment a human might question.

That last one is why the count grows on AI-assisted branches. The tool is not malicious; it is doing exactly what it was asked. The ban list just does not cover the escape hatch it found.

The gate I added

A grep in CI, with an explicit allowlist file — because the goal is not zero this week, it is "never again 117".

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# fail when the double-cast count grows past the recorded budget
budget=$(cat .cast-budget)
actual=$(grep -rn --include='*.ts' --include='*.tsx' \
  --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.next \
  'as unknown as' apps packages | grep -v 'as-unknown-as-allow' | wc -l)

echo "as unknown as: ${actual} (budget ${budget})"
if [ "$actual" -gt "$budget" ]; then
  echo "New double casts. Narrow the type, or add the line to the allowlist with a reason."
  exit 1
fi

Three properties matter more than the rule itself:

  • A budget, not a ban. A hard zero on day one means a 117-line allowlist nobody reads. A ratchet — budget goes down when you fix one, never up — keeps the number honest.
  • The allowlist carries a reason. // as-unknown-as-allow: stripe webhook payload is validated upstream is a reviewable sentence. An empty allowlist entry is a comment that says nothing.
  • It runs in the same job as typecheck, so the count is visible in the PR that changes it.

If your setup has typescript-eslint installed, the equivalent rule is a restricted-syntax selector:

'no-restricted-syntax': ['error', {
  selector: 'TSAsExpression > TSUnknownKeyword',
  message: 'Double cast. Narrow with a parser or a guard instead.',
}]

I would still keep the grep: it works in repos with no ESLint, in CI scripts, and on the day the parser plugin upgrades and the selector stops matching.

The three patterns behind 90% of them

Reading the 117 by hand, they fall into three groups, each with a replacement that costs about ten minutes per file:

1. Parsing external data. JSON.parse(body) as unknown as JobRow becomes a schema parse at the boundary, and everything downstream is genuinely typed:

const JobRow = z.object({ id: z.string(), status: z.enum(['queued', 'running', 'done']) });
const row = JobRow.parse(JSON.parse(body)); // typed, and it fails loudly on drift

2. Reading database rows into a domain type. The cast moves the failure from "somewhere later, with a stack trace that does not mention the column" to "here, at the read". A small mapper function per table beats a cast per caller.

3. Indexing a translation map by a computed key. messages[key] as unknown as string usually wants satisfies Record<Locale, string> on the definition and a typed accessor — the cast disappears because the shape was always there, just unproven.

When the double cast is fine

  • Test doubles. A partial implementation of a large interface is a cast-shaped problem; keep it in tests and let the budget ignore *.test.ts.
  • Module augmentation for untyped third-party packages. You are asserting something the package should have declared. Put it in one types/ file with a comment, and it never needs to appear twice.
  • Migration boundaries. When a column changes type, one cast with a // migration: remove after 2026-12 marker is cheaper than a parallel type tree.

Everything else is a parser you did not write yet.

FAQ

Is as unknown as slower at runtime? No. TypeScript erases both casts; the cost is entirely in what the compiler stops checking.

Does satisfies replace it? Sometimes. satisfies proves a value matches a type without widening it — which is exactly the i18n case — but it cannot rescue a value you did not construct.

Why not ban it outright? Because a ban without a migration path produces an allowlist longer than the problem. The budget is the migration path.

Would a stricter tsconfig catch these? noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes remove a chunk of the reasons people reach for a cast. They also produce a lot of red on day one. Ratchet the same way.

The counts above came from one repository and one grep; your ratio will differ, and the interesting number is the ratio, not the total. If you run the same audit and get zero double casts, I want to know what your boundaries look like, because that is a codebase with parsers everywhere.

articles.title: Séance Shell: A Local Ghost That Haunts Your Terminal
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine    ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Séance Shell is a haunted terminal. A small ghost lives in your Bash or Zsh session, watches for the moments that matter, and murmurs a single eerie sentence about what just happened.

It reacts to two kinds of events:

  • Destructive-looking commands like git reset --hard, git clean -fd, or rm
  • Failed builds and tests like pytest, npm run build, or cargo build

Once the command has finished, the ghost speaks:

$ git reset --hard HEAD~1
ghost: the past has accepted your changes, and forgotten your future.

That's the whole product. The ghost is a companion for reflection, not an assistant for execution. It never suggests commands, never runs anything, and never offers advice.

How I read the theme: the prompt suggested "a haunted terminal that possesses your shell and whispers back eerie commentary." I wanted that, but with restraint. Most AI tools are loud and eager to help. A good ghost lingers at the edge of the room, says one unsettling thing, and goes quiet. Séance Shell is a ghost that knows its place.

Code

0shuvo0 / seance-shell

Séance Shell 👻

A quiet, local-AI terminal companion that offers one short reflection after selected commands. The ghost is atmospheric, not an assistant: it gives no advice, runs no generated text, and never retries a command.

$ git reset --hard HEAD~1
ghost: the past has accepted your changes, and forgotten your future

Reflections are generated independently by Ollama on your machine with gemma3:latest. Model output is validated before display. If the local model is unavailable, the reflection is skipped.

What it does

  • Notices selected destructive-looking commands and failed build/test commands.
  • Reflects only after the shell has already completed a command; it never re-runs it.
  • Sends Ollama a category, outcome, and—only for an explicit seance reflect --context request—short sanitized context. Shell hooks do not send the command text to the model.
  • Requires one sentence, at most 15 words and 180 characters; malformed output is discarded.
  • Uses dim terminal text when…
View on GitHub

To run it locally you need Ollama and the gemma3:latest model. The shell hook works without the model, so the ghost only goes silent if Ollama isn't running.

How I Built It

The open-source pieces are what make this work:

  • Ollama runs inference locally.
  • Gemma 3 (gemma3:latest), Google's open-weight model, is the default.
  • A Bash/Zsh hook detects events after the shell has finished a command.

No cloud API, no hosted inference, no account. Three design decisions shaped the build.

1. The model never sees your command

The shell doesn't send the raw command string to the model. It sends a structured description:

  • category: destructive or failed-build
  • status: succeeded or failed
  • context: optional, and sanitized first

The model gets enough to set a mood but nothing it could be tricked by or leak. It is not a coding agent and can't be steered by arbitrary shell content.

2. The output is validated aggressively

The model is asked for one sentence, at most 15 words and 180 characters. If the response is malformed, multi-line, or too long, it's discarded and the ghost stays silent. The text on screen is a constrained artifact, not whatever the model felt like saying.

3. A ghost, not an agent

Séance Shell never retries commands, never executes anything, and never reinterprets what you did. It's a passive observer. That modesty is what makes it usable in a place where you're making decisions at speed.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A terminal is about as personal as software gets. It holds your file paths, repo names, half-finished experiments, and the commands you'd rather not explain. An always-on ghost watching that is only acceptable if it lives on your own machine.

Open-weight models made that possible in three ways:

  • It works with the lights off. There is no network call in the loop, so the ghost haunts you on a plane, in a basement, or during an outage.
  • Your context stays on your machine. Even with command text withheld, I wouldn't want a terminal's activity flowing to a server I don't control. With a local model I don't have to take anyone's word for it, and I can read exactly what gets sent.
  • I control the personality. The ghost's voice depends on the prompt, the validation rules, and the model. With open weights I can swap Gemma for another model or tighten the constraints without asking a vendor, and nothing can be deprecated out from under it.

A closed API could have written the sentences. It couldn't have given me a ghost that is private, offline, and mine, and that's the part that makes it feel like a haunting rather than a service.

The Spirit of It

The first time it fired, I ran git reset --hard HEAD~1 on a throwaway branch and the ghost answered: "the past has accepted your changes, and forgotten your future." It was a small moment, but the one-line reminder that I had just erased something did what no warning dialog ever has. It made me pause.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 3 runs locally through Ollama as the model behind every one of the ghost's reflections.

articles.title: How nice it is to talk — BeeDialogue lands in BeeEngine 2.11.0
articles.description: Hi. I'm Antonio. I'm 53. I build things out of pure passion.  I don't talk much. But when I do…...
articles.body_html:
Hi. I'm Antonio. I'm 53. I build things out of pure passion.

I don't talk much. But when I do… BeeDialogue comes out.

From “dialogue” to a dialogue plugin

BeeEngine is a small 2D HTML5 Canvas engine I keep shaping in the open. Physics, scenes, sprites, tiles, audio buses, an inventory plugin, a locale plugin. Useful pieces. Quiet pieces.

What was missing for story-shaped games was obvious: a place for NPCs to say something without me inventing a new if tree every weekend.

So v2.11.0 adds BeeDialogue.

Not a chatbot. Not a voice synthesizer. A dialogue tree: speakers, lines, branching choices, straight-line advances. The kind of thing you wire to a blue rectangle that pretends to be a guide on a bridge.

The engine stays blind (on purpose)

BeeEngine has a plugin contract I take seriously. The core does not import plugins. A plugin attaches itself.

import { BeeEngine } from 'beeengine';
import { BeeDialogue, BeeLocale } from 'beeengine/plugins';

const game = new BeeEngine('c', 800, 480);
const locale = new BeeLocale({ /* strings… */, engine: game });

const dialogue = new BeeDialogue({ engine: game, locale, cancelKey: 'Escape' });
// attach() registers it as 'dialogue' — detach() unregisters

No monkey-patch of loop(). No hijacking of update / render. BeeDialogue has no tick of its own and no DOM listeners. Your scene calls the verbs:

  • handleInput(input) from scene.update
  • draw(ctx) from scene.draw (screen space, after the camera)

The motor stays a motor. The plugin stays a plugin. I sleep better.

A tree you can read

You load a tree once. Nodes can be an array (easier to skim) or a map. Literal text / speaker work. Or textKey / speakerKey if you pass an optional BeeLocale (constructor, setLocale, or engine.plugin('locale')).

dialogue.load({
  start: 'intro',
  nodes: [
    {
      id: 'intro',
      speakerKey: 'guide',
      textKey: 'hi',
      choices: [
        { textKey: 'ask_map', next: 'map', data: { topic: 'map' } },
        { textKey: 'bye', next: null, data: { topic: 'bye' } }
      ]
    },
    { id: 'map', speakerKey: 'guide', textKey: 'map', next: 'tip' },
    { id: 'tip', speakerKey: 'guide', textKey: 'tip' }
  ]
});

Rules that saved me from myself:

  • Node without choices → advance() follows next (or ends).
  • Node with choices → choose(index).
  • The wrong verb returns false and warns. Good. I need warnings more than cleverness.
  • start() while already open does a clean restart (end with reason restart, then start again).

Drawing choices (without becoming a second renderer)

BeeDialogue is not BeeText.drawHUD. It draws a simple panel when you ask.

const scene = {
  update(_dt, input) {
    if (input.wasPressed('KeyE') && !dialogue.isOpen()) dialogue.start();
    dialogue.handleInput(input); // Space / Enter advances or confirms; arrows move the highlight
  },
  draw(ctx) {
    dialogue.draw(ctx, { x: 40, width: ctx.canvas.width - 80 });
  }
};

onChange reports start, node, choice, advance, and end (with a reason: finished, cancel, restart, reload, missing-node…). Enough to feed a future quest plugin without hard-wiring anything today.

And yes — toJSON / fromJSON save the tree and where you stood, so you can tuck the DTO into BeeSave next to inventory slots. Definitions stay yours; restore reopens on the saved node and emits node (not a fake second start).

About that demo label

The demo is examples/dialogue.html. Press E.

The English string does not say “E to talk”.

It says “E to interact”.

Because BeeDialogue does not talk. It does not clear its throat. It does not do regional accents. It advances nodes. The joke writes itself, and I left it in the locale table on purpose (talk: 'E to interact'). Press L if you want Italian. The guide still will not speak aloud. She will, however, mention a village east of a bridge, which is already more social than most of my week.

Why this shape

I like small contracts:

Piece Job
BeeLocale t(key) — pure read
BeeInventory stacks, use, equip — no draw loop
BeeDialogue tree state — you draw and feed input

Together they feel like a tiny RPG toolkit without pretending to be one. Next ideas on the shelf (one at a time): Quest, Post FX, scene Transition, action remapping… Lights, Spine, Net later. Those touch more surface area. Dialogue was the polite guest who hangs its coat on attach and leaves with detach.

Try it

  • Repo: BeeEngine-V2.5.0 (package beeengine 2.11.0)
  • Demo: examples/dialogue.html
  • Tests: node scripts/test-beedialogue.mjs
  • Import: import { BeeDialogue } from 'beeengine/plugins'

If you break it, tell me how. If you use it in a jam game with three lines of dialogue and a torch tip, tell me that too. Short messages welcome — I don't talk much.

But when I do… you already know what comes out.

— Antonio

articles.title: I got rejected from 50 jobs. Then I deleted everything on my resume except one story — and the callbacks started.
articles.description: For about two months, the first thing I did every morning was refresh an inbox, looking for a word...
articles.body_html:
For about two months, the first thing I did every morning was refresh an inbox, looking for a word that wasn't there.

"Unfortunately." "We've decided to move forward with other candidates." "While your background is impressive." I could recite the rejection template from memory because I'd received roughly fifty versions of it. Some took three weeks. Some took an automated four minutes. A few never came at all, which is somehow the worst one.

And every time, I did the same thing: I opened my resume and made it more. Added the side project I'd shipped that weekend. Added a line for the framework I'd just learned. Bumped "familiar with" up to "proficient in." Reordered the skills so the hot one was first. Rewrote the summary at the top for the fourth time. The resume got denser and denser, a tighter and tighter brick of everything I had ever built.

Fifty applications. Roughly a dozen rewrites. Exactly zero callbacks.

And then, in a single week, it stopped being zero — not because I added a better project, a cleaner layout, or a stronger keyword. Because I deleted almost the entire thing and replaced it with one story. I want to tell you exactly what that story was, because it rewired how I think about my whole career, and it's the opposite of every "add more projects to your portfolio" post you've ever scrolled past.

The thing my resume actually was

Here's the uncomfortable reframe, and it took me fifty rejections to see it.

For two months, my resume was a list of output. "Built a full-stack app with X." "Shipped a feature that does Y." "Used these fourteen technologies." Every bullet was a real, true thing I had typed into existence. None of it was a lie. It was an honest, complete inventory of everything I had produced.

And output — the building, the shipping, the "I made a thing that exists" — is the part that got free. I was writing most of that code with an AI by then, spinning up a polished side project in a weekend. So was every other person applying to the same job. The hiring manager was looking at a stack of resumes that were all, functionally, the same wall of output, generated at roughly the same near-zero cost. Half of them were probably written by the same AI I was using.

A list of things you built is exactly as scarce as the ability to build them. Which is to say: not scarce at all anymore.

Because the thing standing between me and a callback was never another project. I kept treating the rejections as a volume problem — not enough shipped, not enough keywords, not enough proof-of-work — when it was never a volume problem at all. The hard part of hiring someone was never "can they produce code." It's "can I trust this person with the thing that can hurt us." I had compressed the easy part — making things exist — to almost nothing, and spent two months frantically doing more of it, while the part that actually gets people hired sat untouched at the top of the page in a summary nobody read.

I wasn't building a case for myself. I was building a very thorough inventory of a commodity.

The one thing I changed

I almost didn't send it. It felt insane. I cut the fourteen technologies down to a quiet line. I cut three of the four side projects. I cut the summary entirely. And in the space that opened up, I wrote about the single worst night of my short career.

Months earlier, on a tiny app a handful of real people actually used, I had shipped a bug. A write path that acknowledged the request before it had actually persisted the row. In my tests, in the demo, on my machine — flawless. It had been "flawless" for months precisely because no real weight had ever been on it.

Then one user leaned their weight on it. A retry hit at the wrong moment. The ack went out — saved! — and the save never landed. That person got locked out of their own account, with no record that they'd done the thing they'd just spent an evening doing. Ack-before-persist. Their work, gone, and the app cheerfully telling them it was fine.

The message came in late. It was furious, and it was right to be furious.

So on the resume, instead of a bullet that said "built and maintained a production web app," I wrote what actually happened: I found the bug, I understood why it was invisible for months, I fixed the write path so the acknowledgement could not possibly go out before the row was durably written, I recovered what data I could, and I replied to that person — not a templated apology, the real thing: here's what broke, here's why, here's exactly what I changed, here's what I could get back and what I couldn't.

One story. The one time something I built could hurt a real person, and what I did when it did.

Why one story beat fifty lists

The first recruiter who called opened with it. Not my stack. Not my projects. "Tell me more about the ack-before-persist thing."

Here's the line I wish someone had put in front of me on rejection number one:

A resume is a list of output. Output is free now. What gets hired is judgment — proof you can be trusted with the thing that can hurt them.

My fourteen technologies proved nothing, because fourteen technologies cost nothing to list and almost nothing to acquire. They couldn't lock a user out, lose someone's data, or get a 2am message. They were safe, which is exactly why they were worthless on the page — I was handing over proof I could do the free part, in a stack of resumes all proving the same free part.

The one story was the first thing on the page that showed I'd ever been in the room where something could go wrong on a real person — and that when it did, I didn't hide, didn't template, didn't ship away from it. That's not something you can generate. That's the one thing they were actually screening for the whole time, buried under everyone's identical wall of output.

That's the math nobody prints on the "build more projects" advice: fifty resumes full of output got me zero callbacks. One story about judgment got me the job.

To be clear — this is not "projects don't matter"

I need to be fair here, because the lazy version of this post is "stop building side projects," and that's wrong.

I am not telling you to stop building. Build constantly. Ship the side projects. Let an AI write most of the code — I do, it's the reason I could ship enough to have a worst night to write about. The projects are table stakes; you need them to get in the door at all. Building is fast and cheap and good, and you should do it.

What I'm saying is narrower and, I think, more useful: projects were never the bottleneck, so adding more of them was never going to move a number that was stuck for a completely different reason. The scarce thing — the only thing that was ever going to turn a rejection into a callback — was evidence of judgment: proof that I'd depended-on and been depended-on, broken something that mattered, and owned it. AI made the output free and did absolutely nothing about that. It can't. Nobody can generate your scar tissue for you.

So build. Build fast, with the machine. But know which part of your resume is the free part, and do not mistake fourteen lines of the free part for a case that you should be hired.

Why this is the exact reason I build the way I do now

Here's the part that goes one level up, because it's the same lesson wearing a different hat.

I build an agent platform now, and I read resumes and diffs from the other side of the table. The whole industry's reflex this year is to celebrate the author — the thing that generates. Look how much it ships! A whole app in a weekend, a resume in a prompt! But a wall of author output, with nothing checking it, tells me exactly what my fifty-rejection resume told those recruiters: that you can produce. I already assume you can produce. Everyone can produce now.

So when I read a candidate — or review a change — I'm not scanning for more output. I'm hunting for the skeptic and the human. The author is the part that writes the code, fast and tireless and free. The skeptic is the part that asks the question I didn't ask for months: what does this do if the write gets retried? And the human is the one who owns the 2am, who can see the blast radius the model can't. Author, skeptic, human. That separation is the entire shape of xenition — and it's the same thing fifty rejections taught me the hard way: generating the thing is free and always will be; being trustable with it when it can hurt someone is the whole job, and the only part anyone ever pays for.

My resume didn't get rejected fifty times because it was missing a project. It got rejected because it was all author and no skeptic, all output and no judgment, and nothing on it had ever been close enough to a real person to go wrong. The day one line finally was — and I'd stood in it — the number changed.

Put one thing on your resume that could have hurt someone. Then show them you stayed. That's where the callback is.

articles.title: Halls of Horror: Build a Haunted House with Gemma, Then Dare Your Friends to Walk It
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine    ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

I've always treasured Halloween. It's my favorite holiday. My dad and I share the same love for Halloween - I definitely inherited the love from him. I mean, there is a reason why I have Freddy and Jason tattoos!

I remember going to Netherworld for the first time back in college, 16 years ago. It was my first haunted house! I've gone almost every year since. I went to a few different haunted houses but nothing beats the best. I am so fond of it. The art. I view haunted houses as the ultimate art form. Netherworld just knocks it out of the park each year. They are the true masterminds of the art of Halloween.

I'm truly sad to miss this year because I’m recovering from ankle surgery but I will be back next year!

I wanted to build an app as an homage to my love for haunted houses and storytelling.

So I built Halls of Horror: a haunted house builder where Gemma, running right in your browser, is the creative director.

  • Pick your nightmare: an abandoned asylum, a carnival that never left town, a hotel with a sealed 13th floor, a toy shop after dark… or dream up your own
  • Choose how scary: Cozy creepy, Creepy or Terrifying
  • Gemma builds the haunt: the legend guests hear in line, then room after room of what they see, what they hear, the scare and the scare actor's line
  • A secret 13th room: behind the last room waits a locked door, with a twist ending you only see at the very end
  • Walk it: a dark, flickering hallway, room by room, with a flashlight that follows your mouse and creepy sound made live in your browser. No audio files at all.
  • Every character screams their own way: the ghost wails, the doll giggles, the clown laughs, the witch cackles, the shadow growls, the captain moans and the bellhop rings his bell
  • Sound captions: every scream, the thunder and the 13th door show up as text, so the scares work on mute too
  • Survive it: make it out and you get a card with the rooms you walked, the scares you survived, and whether you found the secret room, plus a button to share the haunt
  • Share it: send a link and your friends can walk your haunt, no download needed
  • Print the actor script: every room as a script for real scare actors. Home haunters, this one's for you.

How I read the theme: "Ghost in the Machine" is the ghost writer living in your browser. Gemma dreams up the haunt, and the walk-through puts you inside it.

Demo

Live app: https://halls-of-horror.onrender.com (Chrome or Edge on a laptop works best. Click "walk through a sample haunt" to try the walk-through without downloading Gemma.)

Code

tmott13 / halls-of-horror

🕯️ Gemma builds you a walk-through haunted house, right in your browser. Pick a theme, get a legend, rooms full of scares, and a secret 13th room. Painted scenes, a flashlight mode, character screams, and sound captions. No server, no sign-up. Built with Angular + WebLLM.

Halls of Horror

Build a walk-through haunted house with Gemma. Then dare your friends to walk it.

Pick a nightmare (an abandoned asylum, a carnival that never left town, a hotel with a sealed 13th floor…), choose how scary, and Gemma, running right in your browser, writes your haunt: the legend guests hear in line, then room after room of what they see, what they hear, the scare and the scare actor's line. Behind the last room waits a locked 13th door with a twist ending.

Then take the walk-through: a dark, flickering hallway, room by room, with creepy sound made live in your browser (no audio files). Share a link and your friends can walk it too, no download needed.

Live: halls-of-horror.onrender.com · Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

How it works

  1. Design: pick a theme (or dream up your…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

  • Open model: Gemma 2 2B (gemma-2-2b-it-q4f16_1-MLC) on laptops, with Gemma 3 1B as the lighter option for phones.
  • Runs in the browser: WebLLM runs Gemma on your GPU with WebGPU. It downloads once and is cached, so building works offline.
  • Sound: all synthesized with the Web Audio API: a low drone, wind, heartbeats, creaks, a detuned music box, a carnival waltz, and a different scream for each character.
  • Frontend: Angular 22 with signals, plus the Creepster and Special Elite fonts.
  • Hosting: a free static site on Render, with no backend at all.

Like my last four projects, the big idea is Gemma writes the words, and the app owns everything else:

  1. One room at a time. A 2B model loses the thread if you ask for a whole haunted house at once. So Gemma builds one room at a time, and each one sees the legend and the rooms before it. They stay on theme and never repeat.
  2. A simple format the app can always read. Gemma answers in ROOM / SEE / HEAR / SCARE / LINE. The app reads it even when Gemma adds bold or numbers, and fills in anything missing, so a room never breaks.
  3. The app picks the sound. If Gemma writes about a calliope, the room gets the carnival organ. Dripping water gets drips, whispers get whispers. Gemma never touches the audio.
  4. The twist is its own step. The secret 13th room gets its own prompt: it sees every room and has to flip the legend.
  5. Spooky, not gory. Every prompt asks for PG-13 haunted-house fun: no gore, no real people, no real tragedies. And before you enter, a warning screen lets you turn off sound or flashing light. Flashing starts off for anyone who prefers reduced motion.

I was surprised how well Gemma created the script for the haunted houses. A true mix of storytelling and spook.

I built this with Claude as my pair programmer. I picked the idea, made the product calls, and tested every haunt myself.

Accessibility

Accessibility is very important to me, which is why I included some methods inside Halls of Horror.

  • A content warning before you enter, with switches for sound, flashing light and the flashlight
  • Sound captions for every scream, the thunder and the door, read out by screen readers too
  • Reduced motion: the shaking, lunging and flickering turn off, and the scares just fade in and out
  • Keyboard friendly: Space, Enter or → to keep walking, Esc to leave
  • Labeled buttons that say whether they're on or off
  • Your choices are remembered
  • A tap finishes the typing so you never wait

Spoiler alert: I will be creating a series soon called Vibe Check. A series on how AI misses the mark on accessibility and how humans are still needed "in the loop". I will also be making some updates to include more accessibility features and attributes to the projects I created for Hacktoberfest this month.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • It runs anywhere, even offline. Once Gemma is downloaded, you could plan a haunt in a basement with no signal, which feels right.
  • It's private. Your haunts are saved in your browser. Even the share link is the haunt, packed into the part of the link after #, which browsers never send to a server.
  • It's free. No API bill and no subscription, so home haunters and families can play with it all October.
  • It won't disappear. No service to shut down. The model, the code and your haunts are all yours.
  • I control the whole pipeline. I decide what Gemma sees, how it's broken into steps, and the safety rules around it.

The Spirit of It

In the spirit of Halloween, I hope this brings you a spark of joy or even a scare! I loved being able to share my love for Halloween with you! I enjoyed being able to combine my passions of tech, art, and storytelling together with my favorite holiday.

Prize Categories

  • Gemma: Gemma 2 2B and Gemma 3 1B run fully in the browser with WebLLM, writing the legend, every room and the secret 13th room.
  • Render: deployed as a free Render static site from a render.yaml blueprint.

Thanks to DEV, the Hacktoberfest team, and the MLC/WebLLM and Gemma teams. Happy Halloween!

articles.title: I Wanted Real Native UI in My WebView. So I Built Projection. [Capacitor/Cordova]
articles.description: When you build a WebView app with Capacitor or Cordova, you often recreate native UI on the web to...
articles.body_html:
When you build a WebView app with Capacitor or Cordova, you often recreate native UI on the web to make the app feel at home on the device.

I've spent more than a year working on this, releasing my work as an open-source Ionic Theme that recreates native UI with web technologies.

But did I really recreate Liquid Glass, introduced in iOS 26? That's harder to answer. I could get the appearance close, but the background refraction and the way it responds to touch were beyond what I could reproduce on the web.


Both show a long press. Look at the edges of the glass and the background showing through it.

Then why not use real native UI?

That brought me to a different problem: making it coexist with the WebView. Web content and native UI live in separate rendering layers. I couldn't make them feel like one natural interface.

Recently, I found a way. Take a look!

As I slowly close this web-based sheet modal, a native tab bar emerges from underneath it.

The web modal appears above the native tab bar. Close it, and the tab bar is interactive native UI again.

This tab bar isn't an HTML or CSS recreation. It's real native UI rendered by UIKit on iOS.

I call this approach Projection.

The boundary a WebView can't cross

A WebView and native UI don't share a stacking order or a scrolling system.

The WebView renders HTML and CSS. No matter how high you set a CSS z-index, a web modal cannot cover a native view placed above the WebView itself.

Scrolling has the same problem. When content inside the WebView scrolls, a native view doesn't automatically move with it. To place native ads between posts, as you see in an X feed, you need to synchronize their positions—and clip the parts that pass behind the header.

They're separate rendering systems. Of course they behave differently.

But to the person using the app, it's all one screen.

If native UI can't go into the DOM, project its appearance

The turning point was thinking about when native UI can't be interacted with.

When a modal is open, you can't use the tab bar it covers. The same goes for an alert: you can't tap the components behind it.

So, while that UI is unavailable for interaction, does it actually need to stay in the native layer?

Turn it into an image temporarily and place it within the WebView's stacking order. When it becomes interactive again, bring back the real native UI.

The same idea works for scrolling. Switch to an image when scrolling starts, then back to the real view when it stops. Web content and native UI can coexist without compromising the user experience at all.

That realization was pretty exciting.

The native UI itself doesn't need to be in the DOM. Only its appearance does.

That's the idea behind Projection.


In the middle, the tab bar is an image.

In practice, there are three ways to display the UI:

Mode What it shows
Live Native UI The real native view, ready for interaction.
Web Projection An image of the native UI inside a DOM container.
Web Fallback HTML or another fallback supplied by the plugin when an image isn't available.

Of course, you can't interact with the native UI while it's projected as an image. That makes the timing of the switch—in both directions—essential.

It feels like magic

The idea was simple. Getting the handoff right was hard.

Hide the native UI before showing its image, and you get a blank frame. Show the image before hiding the native UI, and the translucent UI appears twice, layered over itself.

Neither works.

So I capture the image on the native side and decode it on the web side during idle time, before the switch. But a UI element can still be changing shape just after a long press ends. On iOS, I check its position and size at intervals roughly equal to one frame at 60fps, and capture it only after three consecutive checks find no change.

When Projection starts, I temporarily show the same image on the native side to bridge the handoff. I place the image, captured with its background, and hide the real native UI in the same native-side operation. This prevents both the blank gap and the doubled translucent UI.

Then I show the image on the web side and use requestAnimationFrame to notify the native side to remove its temporary copy. The appearance stays the same. Only the rendering layer changes.

Just watching the screen, you can't tell when the native UI becomes an image.

It feels like magic!

I've also tuned scrolling separately on iOS and Android so the native UI follows the content smoothly.


Watch the top edge of each ad. On both platforms, it disappears behind the header.

And you can use it today

The first things I wanted to support were iOS navigation—toolbar buttons and a tab bar—and native ads that scroll within web content.

This approach is already available in @rdlabo/capacitor-native-ui and @capacitor-community/admob.

But keeping it limited to the plugins I work on felt like a missed opportunity.

Toolbars, mini-player controls, UI provided by native SDKs—there must be more places where this could help.

So I extracted the shared pieces into WebView Native UI Engine, an open-source library under the MIT license.

It's for Capacitor and Cordova plugin authors, with support for iOS and Android.

Register a native view and its destination DOM container, then notify the Engine of the relevant state changes. It coordinates the display transitions. I designed it to fit into existing plugins while preserving their APIs and business logic.

I'd love for you to try it in one of two ways.

If you build plugins

Whether you're building a new plugin with native UI or extending an existing one, try integrating the Engine.

The Getting Started guide includes a minimal setup and integration instructions.

If you use plugins

Wouldn't it be interesting to have this in a plugin you already use?

Suggest it to the plugin's author. Or, if you think you can implement it, send a pull request.

There must be uses for this that I'd never think of on my own.

I can't wait to see what you build with it!

WebView Native UI Engine on GitHub

articles.title: Five Times the Monster on the Client's Site Was Me
articles.description: Everyone posts haunted house stories today. Mine are less atmospheric. In every one of them, the...
articles.body_html:
Everyone posts haunted house stories today. Mine are less atmospheric. In every one of them, the thing that broke the client's site was me.

Here are five, in no particular order of shame.

1. "It's live, check it out"

I sent the client a message saying the changes were done. The client opened the site and saw the old version.

The cache was holding on to the old site, and I was holding on to the belief that I had deployed. Only one of us was right.

2. Lorem ipsum, live and in production

Placeholder text is supposed to be replaced before anyone sees it. Mine made it onto the live site.

3. It ran fine on my phone

I checked the mobile version on my own phone, saw it working, and moved on. The client opened it on an older phone and it fell apart. Turns out "works on my phone" is just "works on my machine" with a smaller screen.

4. The animation that ate the battery

It looked great on my laptop, smooth and exactly what I wanted.

On a phone it heated the device and drained the battery.

5. The environment variables that weren't there anymore

I overwrote the environment variables on production. Yes, the real ones.

None of these needed a full moon. Just me, convinced it was fine.

What's the scariest thing you've shipped yourself?

articles.title: Stop Hardcoding Color Variants. Relative Color Syntax Does It.
articles.description: A design system ships one brand color and four hand-picked hex variants for hover, pressed, border, and tint. Change the brand color and four of those five silently go stale. CSS relative color syntax derives every variant from the one color you actually update.
articles.body_html:
The PR comment was two words: "wrong blue." Not a bug report, not a reproduction — a designer scrolling through a staging build, stopping on the "Upgrade" button's hover state, and flagging it because something about it felt off against the rest of the rebrand that had shipped two weeks earlier.

They were right, and it took longer than it should have to find out why. The button's resting color matched the new brand blue exactly — that token had been updated the day the rebrand landed. Its hover color was still the old brand blue, darkened. Nobody had touched it, because nobody remembered it existed.

Five variables, one of which actually gets updated

Open almost any design system's color file and you'll find the same shape: one brand color, and a handful of hand-picked variants sitting next to it that all look derived but are actually just... more hex codes.

:root {
  --brand: #3b6fd6;
  --brand-hover: #2f58ab;      /* "a bit darker" — picked by eye, once */
  --brand-active: #244289;     /* "darker still" — same deal */
  --brand-border: #6e92e1;     /* "a bit lighter" */
  --brand-tint: rgba(59, 111, 214, 0.08); /* "faint background wash" */
}

Every one of those four extra values is somebody's good-faith attempt, at some point in the past, to eyeball a lighter or darker or more-transparent version of --brand. They're not wrong on day one. The problem shows up the day --brand changes and the other four don't — because CSS has no idea they were ever related. To the engine, --brand-hover isn't "darker --brand." It's just a string that starts with #2f58ab, full stop.

The "obvious" fix is discipline: a comment reminding whoever edits --brand to also update the other four, or a design-tokens build step that regenerates them from a single source before CSS ever sees them. Both work, right up until the person making a one-line brand tweak six months from now doesn't know the build step exists, or skims past the comment. Discipline that depends on nobody being in a hurry isn't a fix — it's a bet, and the rebrand PR is the bet losing.

The variables were never the problem — storing the relationship was

Here's the reframe that matters: --brand-hover was never really an independent color. It was always a function of --brand — "darker, same hue." --brand-tint was always "the same color, 8% opaque." The relationship was real and well understood by whoever first picked those hex codes. What got lost was that the relationship lived in a person's head for thirty seconds and then evaporated, leaving only its one-time output behind, frozen in a stylesheet forever.

What you actually want is for CSS to store the relationship, not just a snapshot of what it once produced — and that's a genuinely new category of thing for CSS to express. For most of CSS's life, a color value was a dead end: #3b6fd6 tells the renderer what to paint, but nothing about where it came from or how to get a cousin of it. color-mix() loosened that slightly — you can blend two colors — but blending two colors isn't the shape of this problem. You don't have two brand colors to mix; you have one color, and you want its lightness turned down a notch while everything else about it stays put.

Before you keep reading: what would you even call the CSS feature that lets you say "same color, just darker"? It's a fair question, because until relatively recently there wasn't a clean answer.

Relative color syntax: read a color's own channels back out

Relative color syntax lets a color function take another color as input and expose that color's own channels as variables you can do math on, right there in the function call:

:root {
  --brand: #3b6fd6;

  /* "same hue and chroma as --brand, just darker" */
  --brand-hover:  oklch(from var(--brand) calc(l - 0.12) c h);
  --brand-active: oklch(from var(--brand) calc(l - 0.20) c h);

  /* "same color, lighter, for a border" */
  --brand-border: oklch(from var(--brand) calc(l + 0.15) c h);

  /* "same color, 8% opaque" */
  --brand-tint: oklch(from var(--brand) l c h / 8%);
}

Read the oklch(from var(--brand) ...) part literally: "take --brand, convert it to OKLCH, and give me three variables back — l for lightness, c for chroma, h for hue." Whatever you write after that is just CSS math on those three numbers (plus an optional alpha after the slash). calc(l - 0.12) means "this color's own lightness, minus 0.12" — not a hardcoded lightness value, a relationship to whatever --brand happens to be right now.

Change --brand to a rebrand's new blue, or swap it entirely for a dark-mode theme, and every line below it recomputes. There's no second hex code to forget, because there is no second hex code — --brand-hover isn't stored anywhere; it's derived, every time the browser needs it, from the one variable a human actually edits.

This isn't OKLCH-only, either. rgb(), hsl(), and color() all support the same from syntax, exposing whichever channels that color space naturally has:

/* rgb()'s own channels: r, g, b (0–255), alpha */
.badge { background: rgb(from var(--brand) r g b / 15%); }

/* hsl()'s own channels: h, s, l, alpha — s and l come back as plain
   numbers (0-100), not percentages, so the math below uses 10, not 10% */
.link:hover { color: hsl(from var(--brand) h s calc(l - 10)); }

OKLCH is usually the better pick for lightness math specifically, because it's designed so that "lightness" tracks perceived brightness consistently across hues — nudging l down by the same amount darkens a yellow and a blue by roughly the same perceived amount. Nudge hsl()'s l channel the same way and the result can feel inconsistent hue to hue, because HSL's lightness was never built to model human perception in the first place.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The one sharp edge: clamp your math

calc(l - 0.12) is honest math, which means it'll happily produce a number outside the range that makes sense. Pick a brand color that's already quite dark, subtract 0.20 from its lightness, and l can go negative — which isn't a color error so much as a "this doesn't mean anything" result, rendered as whatever the browser decides black looks like.

The fix is the same clamp() you'd reach for anywhere else in CSS, wrapped around the channel math:

--brand-hover: oklch(from var(--brand) clamp(0, calc(l - 0.12), 1) c h);

That one change makes the derivation safe for any input color, including ones your design system doesn't control yet — a user-customizable accent color, say, or a brand color read from a CMS. Skip the clamp and the formula only works for colors in roughly the lightness range you tested it against, which defeats a good chunk of the point: a derivation that only works for some inputs is just a more elaborate hardcoded value.

Is this safe to ship, or is it another flag-gated preview?

Safe to ship — but the rollout order isn't what you'd guess. Safari 16.4 (March 2023) was the earliest browser with something, but it was a partial pass at an older draft of the spec with real parsing bugs; that implementation was later replaced, not extended. Chrome and Firefox did the work of actually matching the final spec through 2024 (Firefox in Firefox 128, July 2024), and Safari didn't catch up — bug fixes included — until Safari 18 in September 2024. So for the exact forms used above, Safari was last to ship the behavior this post describes, not first. Either way, that was over two years ago: by now every major evergreen browser has unprefixed, unflagged, spec-correct support, and there's no realistic "but what about X" objection left to raise for a typical modern browser matrix. If your project still has to support browsers from before that window, the fallback is simple and honest: keep writing literal hex variants for those browsers, and layer the relative syntax on top for everyone else — it degrades to "the hardcoded value you already had," not to a broken page.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

The bug wasn't really "someone forgot to update a hex code." It was that the stylesheet never had anywhere to put the fact that --brand-hover meant "darker --brand" — so that knowledge lived in a person's memory instead, with exactly the shelf life you'd expect. Relative color syntax isn't a shorter way to write the same five hex codes. It's a way to stop writing four of them at all.

Where does your own color system still keep that kind of relationship in a comment instead of in the CSS itself?
