articles.title: Are You a Web Developer or a Browser Expert? 7 Tests I Failed Building a Photo Editor That Never Uploads Your Photos
articles.description: Description: On-device AI, WASM threads, target-size compression, inpainting and 3D LUTs in...
articles.body_html:
Description: On-device AI, WASM threads, target-size compression, inpainting and 3D LUTs in a single HTML file. 7 real lessons from building APIC Web.

Most web developers can build a form, fetch an API and center a div.

Browser experts know what the browser refuses to do, what happens on a phone instead of your laptop, and how to ship real software with no server at all.

I found out which one I was while building APIC Web: a free photo editor, background remover, object remover, converter and compressor where your photos never leave your device. No upload queue, no backend, and the whole thing is one HTML file hosted on GitHub Pages.

Every test below is a real bug or design decision from that build. Score yourself honestly. 👇

Test 1: Why did my AI step silently never finish on phones?

APIC runs AI models in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web (WebAssembly). Multi-threaded WASM needs SharedArrayBuffer, and that needs special response headers (COOP/COEP). A plain static host like GitHub Pages doesn't send them, so crossOriginIsolated is false.

On desktop, the runtime usually degrades gracefully. On phones it often doesn't, and the AI step just hangs with no error. The fix was to stop relying on the fallback:

// Static hosts can't send COOP/COEP, so threads aren't available.
// Force the one configuration that behaves the same everywhere.
ort.env.wasm.numThreads = 1;
ort.env.wasm.proxy = false;

const session = await ort.InferenceSession.create(modelBytes, {
  executionProviders: ['wasm'],
  enableCpuMemArena: false,
  enableMemPattern: false,
});

Where headers are available, APIC checks self.crossOriginIsolated before asking for more than one thread.

Developer: "It works on my laptop."
Expert: knows that "falls back gracefully" is a claim to test on a real phone, not a promise.

Test 2: Can you tell a slow download from a dead one?

APIC's AI models are big: 5 MB (Lite), 44 MB (Fast), 176 MB (Maximum) for background removal, and about 208 MB for the highest-quality object remover. A fixed 30-second timeout would kill every slow phone connection.

So the timeout is stall-based: abort only if no bytes arrive for 40 seconds. A huge model on bad Wi-Fi is allowed to take as long as it needs. A dead link is not. After that it goes into the Cache API so the second run is instant:

const CACHE = 'apic-models-v1';
const cache = await caches.open(CACHE);

let hit = await cache.match(url);
if (hit) return hit.arrayBuffer();           // cached: no download

const bytes = await downloadWithStallTimeout(url);   // abort only if the stream goes quiet
await cache.put(url, new Response(bytes));   // wrapped in try/catch: private mode & quota can fail
return bytes;

And if a model can't load at all, the tool steps down instead of failing: Ultra (LaMa) → MI-GAN → a quick patch fill.

Developer: fetch() with a timeout.
Expert: measures progress, caches the result, and always has a plan B.

Test 3: Can your app hit "under 200 KB" without guessing?

Upload forms say "max 200 KB" and users play quality-slider roulette. APIC's Compress tool does a binary search on JPEG quality instead:

async function findQualityForTarget(canvas, targetBytes) {
  let lo = 0.05, hi = 0.98, best = null;
  for (let i = 0; i < 7; i++) {
    const mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    const blob = await toBlob(canvas, 'image/jpeg', mid);
    if (blob.size <= targetBytes) { best = { blob, q: mid }; lo = mid; }  // fits: try higher quality
    else { hi = mid; }                                                   // too big: go lower
  }
  return best;
}

Seven encodes find the highest quality that still fits. If even the lowest quality is too big, APIC shrinks the image by about 20% and searches again, up to 8 times. If it still can't make it, it tells you the real size instead of pretending.

Developer: quality = 0.7 and hope.
Expert: turns a guess into a search and is honest when the answer is "can't".

Test 4: Why did my transparent PNG turn black as a JPEG?

JPEG has no alpha channel. When a canvas with transparent pixels is encoded as JPEG, those pixels come out black. After background removal (which creates lots of transparency), that's a nasty surprise.

The fix is to paint white first, then draw the image on top:

function flattenToWhite(src) {
  const out = document.createElement('canvas');
  out.width = src.width; out.height = src.height;
  const ctx = out.getContext('2d');
  ctx.fillStyle = '#fff';
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, out.width, out.height);
  ctx.drawImage(src, 0, 0);
  return out;
}

APIC also tells you which formats keep transparency (PNG, WebP) and which don't, right in the Convert panel.

Developer: assumes a canvas is just pixels.
Expert: knows every output format has rules about alpha.

Test 5: Do you process the whole image, or only what changed?

Removing an object means running an inpainting model (LaMa, a Fourier-convolution network, or the lighter MI-GAN). LaMa works on a fixed 512×512 window, so feeding it a 12-megapixel photo would be slow and blurry.

APIC only processes the area around your brush:

  1. Take a region around the mask (at least 512 native pixels when the photo allows).
  2. Run the model on just that crop.
  3. Feather the edge with box blurs, colour-match the fill to its surroundings, and re-add film grain so it doesn't look "too clean".
  4. Paste it back.

Small edit, small compute, and the rest of your photo is untouched.

Developer: runs the model on the full image.
Expert: shrinks the problem first, then blends the result back so nobody can see the seam.

Test 6: Can you export your whole colour grade as a .cube LUT?

APIC has curves, an 8-band HSL mixer and 3-way colour grading. People wanted to use those grades in DaVinci Resolve or Premiere. A .cube file is a 3D lookup table: for every input colour, what colour comes out.

The trick: you don't need to reverse-engineer your pipeline. Feed an identity grid of colours through the same pixel function, and write down what comes out:

const N = 33;                       // 33×33×33 lattice
const buf = new Uint8ClampedArray(N * N * N * 4);
let i = 0;
for (let b = 0; b < N; b++)
  for (let g = 0; g < N; g++)
    for (let r = 0; r < N; r++) {   // red changes fastest, as .cube requires
      buf[i++] = Math.round(r / (N - 1) * 255);
      buf[i++] = Math.round(g / (N - 1) * 255);
      buf[i++] = Math.round(b / (N - 1) * 255);
      buf[i++] = 255;
    }

processPixels(buf, gradeWithoutSpatialEffects);   // same code that edits your photo

const lines = ['TITLE "APIC grade"', 'LUT_3D_SIZE 33',
               'DOMAIN_MIN 0.0 0.0 0.0', 'DOMAIN_MAX 1.0 1.0 1.0', ''];
for (let j = 0; j < buf.length; j += 4)
  lines.push(`${(buf[j]/255).toFixed(6)} ${(buf[j+1]/255).toFixed(6)} ${(buf[j+2]/255).toFixed(6)}`);

One catch: a LUT can only hold colour operations. Clarity, sharpen, vignette and grain depend on neighbouring pixels, so they're excluded and the UI says so.

Developer: exports a screenshot of the look.
Expert: samples the function itself.

Test 7: Why does your resized image look soft? 

ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0, smallW, smallH);   // one big jump: soft, aliased

Shrinking a large image in one drawImage call looks muddy. APIC's Resize tool halves the image step by step until it's within 2× of the target, then does one final pass:

function highQualityResize(src, targetW, targetH) {
  let cur = src, w = src.width, h = src.height;
  while (w > targetW * 2 || h > targetH * 2) {
    const nw = Math.max(targetW, Math.round(w / 2));
    const nh = Math.max(targetH, Math.round(h / 2));
    const step = document.createElement('canvas');
    step.width = nw; step.height = nh;
    const c = step.getContext('2d');
    c.imageSmoothingEnabled = true;
    c.imageSmoothingQuality = 'high';
    c.drawImage(cur, 0, 0, nw, nh);
    cur = step; w = nw; h = nh;
  }
  // ...then one last high-quality pass onto the exact target size
}

Developer: drawImage once and move on.
Expert: knows the order of operations changes the result.

Bonus: How do you ship a Web Worker inside a single HTML file?

No build step, no separate worker.js. APIC keeps the worker's source as a string, turns it into a Blob and starts it from a Blob URL:

const SRC = `/* worker code as a string */`;
const worker = new Worker(
  URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([SRC], { type: 'application/javascript' }))
);

Heavy inpainting runs off the main thread, and the whole app is still one file you can host anywhere.

Try it yourself

APIC is built by Akhouri Systems. It runs in your browser, and your images are never uploaded. The only thing the browser downloads is the AI model files (from Hugging Face), cached after the first run. Being upfront about the trade-offs: editing needs no account, you sign in with one tap on Google only when you export, and the web version shows one small banner ad to stay free. The offline PC app has none.

App What it is Lessons it proves Get it
🖼️ APIC Web Edit, pro colour tools, remove objects, remove backgrounds with AI, resize, convert, compress, 15-network social presets, batch ZIP Tests 1-7 Open APIC Web
💻 APIC for PC Windows version, runs fully offline, no account The desktop twin Download (zip)

If you're learning how the browser works outside a tutorial, open it, drop a photo, then open DevTools and see what's going on under the hood. That's the fastest way I know to level up.

Your score

  • 0-2 tests known: You're a web developer. Great start, now break something on a real phone.
  • 3-5: Solid. You've shipped something real.
  • 6-7: You're a browser expert. Come argue with me in the comments.

Which test did you fail first? Mine was [the AI step that worked on desktop and silently hung on phones]. Tell me yours below 👇

articles.title: How I Rebuilt the Homepage of My HTML5 Games Portal (and What I Learned About Caching)
articles.description: I run a free HTML5 games portal, SPC – Super Play Combo. It's built on WordPress with the...
articles.body_html:
I run a free HTML5 games portal, SPC – Super Play Combo. It's built on WordPress with the GeneratePress theme and has over 3,000 games from the GameMonetize and GamePix feeds. Over the last few weeks I rebuilt the homepage in a Poki-like style, with one horizontal row per category. It looked easy. It wasn't.

Here are the real problems I ran into and how I fixed them.

1. Category rows with no duplicates

Each category (Puzzle, Arcade, Match-3, Mahjong, Quiz, Sports, Racing…) has its own page with its own game list. The homepage shows one row per category, built by a script called motore-playcombo.js.

The feeds use English category names, while my site uses Italian ones, so I made a map:

const CATEGORIE_HOME = [
  'puzzle', 'sparabolle', 'arcade', 'match-3', 'mahjong',
  'trivia', 'gamesforgirls', 'sports', 'racing',
  'card', 'adventure', 'platformer', '2048'
];

Golden rule: each game appears in exactly one row. A Set of already-used ids does the job:

const alreadyShown = new Set();

function removeDuplicates(games) {
  return games.filter(g => {
    const key = g.id || g.url || g.title;
    if (alreadyShown.has(key)) return false;
    alreadyShown.add(key);
    return true;
  });
}

Rows further down only load when they're about to scroll into view:

const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  entries.forEach(e => {
    if (e.isIntersecting) {
      loadRow(e.target.dataset.category);
      observer.unobserve(e.target);
    }
  });
}, { rootMargin: '300px' });

2. "It works when I'm logged in, but not in incognito"

The Quiz and Card rows were full when I was logged in as admin, but empty for visitors. The culprit was LiteSpeed Cache. For visitors who aren't logged in, it optimizes the page and turns the game list inside the HTML into base64. My script was looking for plain text and found nothing.

The fix is to try decoding it:

function readList(text) {
  try { return JSON.parse(text); } catch (e) {}
  try { return JSON.parse(atob(text)); } catch (e) {}
  return [];
}

Lesson: always test in incognito. What you see as an admin is not what your users see.

3. The little ?v= number that saves your life

The script is loaded like this:

<script src="/js/motore-playcombo.js?v=16"></script>

?v=16 does nothing to the code. It only tells the browser (and the cache, and the PWA service worker) that the file is new. Every time I upload a new version, I:

  1. bump the number on every page that loads the script;
  2. purge the LiteSpeed cache.

Forget this and you'll get 404 errors for files you already deleted, because the browser is still running the old version. Ask me how I know.

4. Thumbnails: from wsrv.nl to i0.wp.com

To make thumbnails lighter, I was running them through an image proxy. Then I found out that the service's robots.txt blocks Googlebot, so Google couldn't see my images. I switched to WordPress's free image CDN:

function optimizeImg(url) {
  if (url.includes('gamepix') || url.includes('?')) return url;
  const u = new URL(url);
  return `https://i0.wp.com/${u.host}${u.pathname}?w=240&quality=75`;
}

I also added a small safety net: if the optimized image fails to load, it falls back to the original.

img.onerror = () => { img.onerror = null; img.src = original; };

The result is a much faster homepage.

5. A bit of (lightweight) style

One last touch: the background has game-themed icons (a joypad, a coin, a star, a heart) made with pure CSS and no shadows, so phones don't struggle. With body.page-id-XXXX I can give each page its own look, like floating yellow stars only on the Girls page.

Takeaways

  • Always test in incognito and on a phone.
  • The cache is your friend, until you forget about it.
  • A wrong (or unchanged) ?v= can cost you hours.
  • Check the robots.txt of any third-party service you rely on.
  • PWA errors often go away by themselves after a few minutes, so don't panic right away.

If you want to see the result, the games are on playcombo.it. Free, as always. 🎮

articles.title: Node Runs .ts Files Natively. Inside node_modules It Refuses, on Purpose
articles.description: Node strips TypeScript types by swapping them for whitespace. It still refuses .ts files under node_modules, by design. Here's what to ship instead.
articles.body_html:
• Book: TypeScript in Production
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You stop compiling. Your package's exports points straight at ./src/index.ts, every script in the monorepo runs with plain node, and the tests are green. Then someone installs the package from the registry, runs their app, and Node stops with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING.

No flag turns it off. The Node.js TypeScript docs give the reason in one sentence: "To discourage package authors from publishing packages written in TypeScript, Node.js refuses to handle TypeScript files inside folders under a node_modules path."

The refusal makes sense once you see how little Node does to a .ts file.

How Node runs a .ts file without compiling it

Type stripping landed in v22.6.0, became the default in v23.6.0 and v22.18.0, and was marked stable in v25.2.0 and v24.12.0. Current releases of every LTS line on the Node releases page (22, 24 and 26, with v26.13.0 the newest LTS release listed there at the time of writing) have it on by default. You opt out with --no-strip-types.

The mechanism is deliberately dumb. Node doesn't compile anything. It finds the TypeScript syntax and overwrites it with spaces. This is the example from the node:module docs:

import { stripTypeScriptTypes } from 'node:module';
const code = 'const a: number = 1;';
const strippedCode = stripTypeScriptTypes(code);
console.log(strippedCode);
// Prints: const a         = 1;

The = 1 is still in the column where you typed it. An interface that spans twelve lines becomes twelve blank lines. Because nothing moves, a stack trace points at the right line of your .ts file, and the docs note that "source maps are unnecessary for correct line numbers in stack traces; and Node.js does not generate them." The parser doing this is Amaro, a wrapper around SWC's TypeScript parser compiled to WebAssembly.

Being dumb has consequences, and they're all in the docs. There is no type checking. Node ignores tsconfig.json, so paths aliases don't work. Imports need their real extension (./user.ts, not ./user). Type-only imports must say import type, or Node treats them as values and fails at runtime. .tsx is unsupported.


Type stripping removes the annotations and leaves the gaps, so every line and column stays where it was.

The syntax whitespace can't erase

If stripping is "replace with spaces", anything that needs Node to write new JavaScript is out. The Node docs list the main cases: enums, namespaces with runtime code, parameter properties and import aliases. Hitting one throws ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX.

The reason is visible in what tsc emits for them. An enum is a real object at runtime, so the compiler has to generate the code that builds it. A parameter property is shorthand for an assignment the compiler writes into the constructor. Neither exists in your source as JavaScript, so blanking characters can't produce it.

// Rejected by type stripping
class User {
  constructor(public name: string) {}
}

enum Role { Admin, Viewer }

The erasable versions say the same thing in syntax that's already JavaScript once the types are gone:

class User {
  name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
}

const Role = { Admin: 0, Viewer: 1 } as const;
type Role = (typeof Role)[keyof typeof Role];

You don't want to find these one runtime crash at a time. TypeScript 5.8 added erasableSyntaxOnly for exactly this: with it on, tsc errors on enums, namespaces and modules with runtime code, parameter properties, import = and export =. The tsconfig reference adds <number>value-style assertions to the list. The Node docs recommend TypeScript 5.8 or newer with erasableSyntaxOnly, verbatimModuleSyntax and rewriteRelativeImportExtensions turned on.

There used to be an escape hatch. --experimental-transform-types arrived in v22.7.0 and was removed in v26.0.0, along with the transform mode of stripTypeScriptTypes. On Node 26 the built-in path is strip-only. For full TypeScript, the docs point you to a third-party runner such as tsx.

Reproduce the refusal (your monorepo hides it)

Here's a two-package npm workspace where the library ships raw TypeScript:

greet-demo/
├── package.json          "workspaces": ["packages/*"]
└── packages/
    ├── greet-ts/
    │   ├── package.json
    │   └── src/index.ts
    └── app/
        ├── package.json
        └── main.ts

The library's manifest points exports at source:

{
  "name": "greet-ts",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": "./src/index.ts"
}

// packages/greet-ts/src/index.ts
export function greet(name: string): string {
  return `hello, ${name}`;
}

// packages/app/main.ts (app has "type": "module")
import { greet } from "greet-ts";
console.log(greet("ada"));

Run npm install at the root, then node packages/app/main.ts, and it should run. That's because npm symlinks each workspace into node_modules. By default Node dereferences symlinks and uses the module's "real path" as its identity. As Jake Bailey points out in nodejs/typescript#14, the "is this in node_modules" check looks at that real path. So Node sees packages/greet-ts/src/index.ts, with no node_modules anywhere in it, and strips it happily.

Your consumers don't get a symlink. They get a copy. Pack the library the way the registry would and install the tarball somewhere else:

cd ~/code/greet-demo/packages/greet-ts
npm pack
mkdir ~/code/consumer && cd ~/code/consumer
npm init -y
npm install ~/code/greet-demo/packages/greet-ts/greet-ts-1.0.0.tgz

Copy main.ts over as main.mts (.mts always runs as ESM, whatever npm init wrote into type) and run node main.mts. The library's index.ts now lives at node_modules/greet-ts/src/index.ts. That is the case the errors reference describes for ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING: "Type stripping is not supported for files descendant of a node_modules directory." I haven't run this exact repro myself; the error code and its trigger come straight from those docs. npm's install-links setting, which packs file: dependencies (not workspaces) instead of symlinking them, is another way to get the same copy-not-link setup in CI.


A symlinked workspace package resolves outside node_modules and runs. The same files installed from a tarball sit inside node_modules and are refused.

Why Node says no

The request to lift the restriction is nodejs/typescript#14, and it was closed as not planned. The issue's author makes a fair case: Bun, Deno and JSR already run or host TypeScript source, so Node holding out alone won't stop the trend. Replies in the thread explain the other side. Matteo Collina wrote that "TypeScript is designed so that only .d.ts files are shared across projects." Jake Bailey raised the problem that a published .ts file gets type-checked under the consumer's tsconfig, not the author's. Jordan Harband added that, as he understood it, the TypeScript team opposes the idea too, because it would mean they could never make breaking changes to TypeScript's syntax again.

TypeScript's own compiler options guide shows the type-checking cost. A separate outDir is "necessary for libraries that publish their input files. Otherwise, extension substitution will cause the library's consumers to load the library's .ts files instead of .d.ts files, causing type errors and performance problems." Raw .ts in node_modules hands the consumer's compiler your source and your strictness assumptions.

If you control both ends, there is a workaround. One commenter in the thread shares a loader built on module.registerHooks() and stripTypeScriptTypes(), both "release candidate" stability. That loader calls stripTypeScriptTypes() in transform mode, which Node 26 removed, so on current Node the same idea would have to use the default strip mode and handle erasable syntax only. That fits an internal app. It isn't something to ask the users of a public package to install.

What your package still ships

Your own scripts and tests can run the .ts files directly. The thing you publish is still compiled JavaScript plus declarations. One tsconfig covers both, combining the Node recommendations with the library settings from the TypeScript guide:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist"
  }
}

rewriteRelativeImportExtensions (TypeScript 5.7) is what lets one source tree serve both: you write import { x } from "./x.ts", Node runs it as-is, and tsc rewrites it to ./x.js in dist. Then the manifest points at the build output:

{
  "name": "greet-ts",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": {
    ".": {
      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
      "default": "./dist/index.js"
    }
  },
  "files": ["dist"],
  "scripts": { "build": "tsc -p tsconfig.json" }
}

Key order matters in conditional exports: "earlier entries have higher priority," and the types condition "should always be included first." Node doesn't type-check, so keep a tsc --noEmit step in CI.

JSR: the registry that compiles for you

JSR is the one registry where publishing TypeScript source is the expected path. It "supports and encourages publishing TypeScript source code rather than pairs of .js + .d.ts files." The catch is what reaches Node. Through JSR's npm compatibility layer, "this source code is transpiled to JavaScript," and .d.ts files "are generated for all TypeScript files." A Node user who runs npx jsr add, or installs with pnpm 10.9+ or Yarn 4.9+, gets JavaScript in node_modules.

That's also why JSR enforces its "slow types" rule on exported functions, classes and variables: explicit types are what let it generate declarations for the npm layer.

If this was useful

Getting a package from "it runs in my repo" to "it runs in yours" is most of what TypeScript in Production covers: tsconfig choices, build tools, monorepos, exports maps, dual ESM/CJS and publishing to JSR. If your team has started running .ts directly and is wondering what still needs a build, that book is the one to grab.

It's the fifth book in The TypeScript Library:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Books 1 and 2 are the core path. If you're coming from the JVM or PHP, swap in book 3 or 4 for those. Book 5 is for anyone shipping TypeScript at work, which, if you read this far, is probably you.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: strlen Says 4, .length Says 2: PHP Byte Strings vs TypeScript UTF-16 for One Emoji
articles.description: One thumbs-up emoji, four different lengths. Side-by-side PHP and TypeScript for length, slicing, reversing and byte limits, with the fixes.
articles.body_html:
• Book: PHP to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Ask PHP how long a thumbs-up emoji is and strlen says 4. Ask mb_strlen and it says 1. Move the same validation rule to TypeScript and .length says 2. Spread it into an array and you get 1 again. Four answers for one character on the screen. Each function is counting a different unit.

If you are porting PHP to TypeScript, this is one of the first places where code that looks like a line-for-line translation quietly changes behaviour. A "max 280 characters" check, a username truncation, a "reverse this string" helper in a test fixture: each one measures something else after the move. The fixes on the TypeScript side are short once you know which unit you need.

Two languages, two units

PHP's manual is blunt about it: "a character is the same as a byte," and "internally, PHP strings are byte arrays" (PHP manual, Strings). PHP does not know what encoding a string is in. It holds whatever bytes your source file or your request body had, which these days is almost always UTF-8. The strlen docs say it returns "the number of bytes rather than the number of characters."

JavaScript, and so TypeScript, stores strings as UTF-16. MDN defines length as the length of the string "in UTF-16 code units." Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, which includes nearly every emoji, take two code units: a surrogate pair. TypeScript adds nothing here: the string type carries no encoding information, and you get the JavaScript runtime's behaviour.

The thumbs-up is U+1F44D. In UTF-8 it is four bytes, F0 9F 91 8D. In UTF-16 it is the surrogate pair D83D DC4D (Compart, U+1F44D). Those two encodings explain every result below.


Same emoji, two rulers: PHP measures bytes, TypeScript measures UTF-16 code units.

Counting length

Every snippet in this post runs as a one-liner with PHP's CLI (php -r) or Node.js (node -e). Both use the \u{...} escape so you don't have to paste an emoji into your terminal. In PHP's double-quoted strings it writes the code point's UTF-8 bytes (PHP manual, Strings); in JavaScript it writes the UTF-16 code units.

php -r '$s = "\u{1F44D}";
echo strlen($s), " ", mb_strlen($s, "UTF-8"), PHP_EOL;'
# 4 1

node -e 'const s = "\u{1F44D}";
console.log(s.length, [...s].length);'
# 2 1

strlen counts the four UTF-8 bytes. mb_strlen (from the mbstring extension) counts code points, and "a multi-byte character is counted as 1." .length counts the two UTF-16 code units. Spreading the string uses the string iterator, which walks code points, so [...s].length is 1. MDN recommends it when you want a character count.

So mb_strlen and [...s].length agree. Port a PHP length check to that pair, and leave strlen and .length out of it.

Now add a skin tone. 👍🏽 is U+1F44D followed by U+1F3FD, the Fitzpatrick type-4 modifier, itself four UTF-8 bytes F0 9F 8F BD and the surrogate pair D83C DFFD (Compart, U+1F3FD). A reader sees one thumb. Here is what each function sees:

Function 👍 👍🏽 Unit
PHP strlen 4 8 UTF-8 bytes
PHP mb_strlen 1 2 code points
PHP grapheme_strlen 1 1 grapheme clusters
TS .length 2 4 UTF-16 code units
TS [...s].length 1 2 code points
TS Intl.Segmenter 1 1 grapheme clusters

The grapheme row is what a human means by "character." On the PHP side that is grapheme_strlen from the intl extension. On the TypeScript side it is Intl.Segmenter, whose default granularity is "grapheme":

const seg = new Intl.Segmenter();

function graphemeLength(s: string): number {
  return [...seg.segment(s)].length;
}

graphemeLength("\u{1F44D}\u{1F3FD}"); // 1

Create the segmenter once and reuse it. It carries locale data, so building one per call is wasteful.

Cutting a string in half

Truncation is where the counting difference turns into broken data. Cut two units off the front in each language:

php -r 'echo bin2hex(substr("\u{1F44D}", 0, 2)), PHP_EOL;'
# f09f

node -e 'const half = "\u{1F44D}".slice(0, 1);
console.log(half.charCodeAt(0).toString(16));
console.log(half.isWellFormed());'
# d83d
# false

PHP's substr hands you the first two bytes of a four-byte sequence, which is invalid UTF-8. The mb_strcut docs describe exactly this: substr cuts the string between the bytes, which would "result in a malformed byte sequence."

TypeScript's slice(0, 1) gives you a lone high surrogate. isWellFormed() returns false for strings with lone surrogates, and it has been available across browsers since October 2023 (Node 20+ on the server). The same MDN page shows encodeURI throwing URIError: URI malformed on such a string, so a truncated search term can blow up a URL builder far from where the cut happened.

The quieter failure is serialisation. TextEncoder.encode takes a USVString (WHATWG Encoding spec), and converting a string to a USVString replaces lone surrogates with U+FFFD (Web IDL). So the half-emoji goes over the wire as EF BF BD, the replacement character, with no error anywhere. Your PHP backend receives valid UTF-8 that says "�".


substr and slice cut on bytes and code units, wherever the reader's character happens to sit.

The fix in TypeScript is to cut on grapheme boundaries:

const seg = new Intl.Segmenter();

function truncateGraphemes(s: string, max: number): string {
  let out = "";
  let n = 0;
  for (const { segment } of seg.segment(s)) {
    if (n === max) break;
    out += segment;
    n++;
  }
  return out;
}

The PHP equivalent is mb_substr if code points are enough, or grapheme_substr from intl, which counts in grapheme units, if you want the skin tone to stay attached.

Reversing a string

The classic interview helper breaks in both languages, in different ways:

php -r 'echo bin2hex(strrev("\u{1F44D}")), PHP_EOL;'
# 8d919ff0

node -e 'const r = "\u{1F44D}".split("").reverse().join("");
console.log(r.isWellFormed());'
# false

strrev reverses bytes, because the bytes are all PHP sees. 8D 91 9F F0 is not UTF-8. split("") splits into UTF-16 code units, so reversing swaps the two halves of the surrogate pair into an order that no longer forms a pair.

Spreading fixes the single emoji, since [..."\u{1F44D}"] is one element. It does not fix 👍🏽: spreading gives two code points, and reversing them puts the skin-tone modifier in front of the thumb, which usually renders as a colour swatch followed by a default yellow thumb. The grapheme-correct version reuses the segmenter:

function reverseGraphemes(s: string): string {
  return Array.from(seg.segment(s), (x) => x.segment)
    .reverse()
    .join("");
}

PHP 8.4 added grapheme_str_split, so the PHP mirror is implode("", array_reverse(grapheme_str_split($s))).

When the limit is in bytes

Sometimes you really do want PHP's strlen behaviour. Storage and wire limits are often in bytes. MySQL's storage requirements page says VARCHAR(M) counts characters, but binary types count bytes, utf8mb4 needs up to four bytes per character, and every row shares a 65,535-byte maximum. That is why a utf8mb4 VARCHAR tops out at 16,383 characters. A VARBINARY(255) column, a fixed-size protocol field or a header with a byte cap all measure bytes, and .length is the wrong number for every one of them.

In TypeScript, TextEncoder returns a Uint8Array of the UTF-8 bytes, so its length is the number PHP's strlen would give you for the same UTF-8 string:

const enc = new TextEncoder();

enc.encode("\u{1F44D}").length;           // 4
enc.encode("\u{1F44D}\u{1F3FD}").length;  // 8

To truncate to a byte budget without cutting a grapheme, combine the two:

const seg = new Intl.Segmenter();
const enc = new TextEncoder();

function truncateBytes(s: string, maxBytes: number): string {
  let out = "";
  let used = 0;
  for (const { segment } of seg.segment(s)) {
    const size = enc.encode(segment).length;
    if (used + size > maxBytes) break;
    out += segment;
    used += size;
  }
  return out;
}

truncateBytes("ok\u{1F44D}\u{1F3FD}", 5); // "ok"

"ok" is two bytes and the thumb with its skin tone is eight, so a 5-byte budget keeps only "ok". The PHP side already has this as one call: grapheme_extract with GRAPHEME_EXTR_MAXBYTES returns whole grapheme clusters that fit the byte budget. If you only need code-point safety, mb_strcut moves a cut that lands inside a multibyte character back to that character's first byte.

The porting checklist

When a PHP string function crosses into TypeScript, ask which unit the original code meant, not which function has the same shape:

  • strlen used as a byte budget becomes new TextEncoder().encode(s).length.
  • mb_strlen becomes [...s].length.
  • grapheme_strlen, or any "characters as the user sees them" rule, becomes Intl.Segmenter.
  • substr and mb_substr on user text become a grapheme loop, and isWellFormed() is a cheap assertion at the boundary where strings leave your service.

The last one is the guard rail. If a string about to be sent, stored or URL-encoded fails isWellFormed(), something upstream cut it on a code unit, and you'd rather learn that from a failing check than from a "�" in a customer's display name.

If this was useful

Strings are one of the spots where PHP habits carry over to TypeScript without a single type error, which is why they hurt. PHP to TypeScript is the book I wrote for PHP 8+ developers making that move: the sync-to-async shift, generics, discriminated unions, and the runtime differences like this one that the compiler won't flag.

It is one of five in The TypeScript Library. If you are coming from PHP, start with PHP to TypeScript and add The TypeScript Type System when the type system gets interesting. If TypeScript is going to production at work, TypeScript in Production covers the build and tooling side:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

I also build Hermes IDE (GitHub), an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools, so weigh the mention accordingly.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: Five Agents in Split Panes: How xterm.js Draws Text With a WebGL Glyph Atlas
articles.description: Five coding agents streaming into five panes all share one main thread. How xterm.js draws text, DOM vs WebGL, and a benchmark you can run.
articles.body_html:
• Book: System Design Pocket Guide: Interviews
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You split the window five ways. Claude Code is printing a diff in one pane, Codex is running a test suite in another, and a third agent is dumping a 4,000-line build log because you asked it to "check why CI fails." Every one of those panes is a terminal emulator, and in an Electron or Tauri app, or in a browser tab, every one of them is JavaScript drawing characters into the same web page.

Nobody picks an agent setup by asking how the terminal paints glyphs. But when five streams arrive at once, the renderer decides whether the window stays responsive or whether your keystrokes land late. Here is how xterm.js, the terminal component inside VS Code, actually puts text on screen, and a small page you can use to measure it on your own machine.

A terminal is a grid with a 16.6 ms budget

A terminal emulator holds a grid of cells. Each cell has a character, a foreground color, a background color and style flags. Bytes from the process go through a parser that updates the grid, and a renderer turns the visible rows into pixels.

At 60 frames per second you get 16.6 ms per frame for everything on the page's main thread. That number is the budget the VS Code team used when they moved the terminal renderer from the DOM to canvas in 2017, and it still frames the problem.

xterm.js does not redraw on every write. Its RenderDebouncer asks for one requestAnimationFrame and, while that request is pending, widens the dirty range with Math.min on the start row and Math.max on the end row. A thousand writes inside one frame become one render of the rows they touched. Only rows in the viewport get drawn, never the scrollback.

So the renderer's cost is per frame, not per byte. The parser is the part that scales with output. Keep those two apart, because they behave differently when you add panes.

The DOM renderer: spans, layout, garbage

The renderer built into xterm.js core builds HTML. Since xterm.js 6.0 removed the canvas addon, it is that or WebGL. For each dirty row, DomRenderer calls replaceChildren with fresh nodes from DomRendererRowFactory. The factory is careful: it creates one <span> per run of adjacent cells that share background, foreground and style, rather than one per cell. Plain log lines collapse into a few spans per row.

Color-heavy output does not collapse. Agent output is full of ANSI color: green tool names, red diff lines, dim timestamps. Every color change starts a new span. After that the browser has to style, lay out and paint those nodes, and the old nodes become garbage.

The 2017 VS Code post put the ceiling plainly: with a DOM renderer, "performance will always have the hard cap imposed by the layout engine." It also says that composing and laying out the elements "could take longer than a frame (16.6ms) all by itself," and that under heavy output the old renderer dropped "below 10 FPS" (source). That post describes an older DOM renderer, but the shape of the cost is the same: more spans per frame, more layout per frame.


The atlas idea: draw each glyph once into a texture, then copy tiles out of it for every cell that needs that glyph.

The WebGL renderer: rasterise on first use, then copy quads

@xterm/addon-webgl replaces all of that with a WebGL2 renderer. The trick is the glyph atlas.

The first time a cell needs a glyph in a given style, TextureAtlas draws it with the 2D canvas API into a texture page and caches its coordinates. The cache key is the character plus its background, foreground and extended attributes, so a red x and a green x are two entries. Every later cell with that same key is a lookup, not a draw. Pages start at 512 px; when the atlas runs out of page slots, four same-sized pages are merged into one page twice as wide and twice as tall, as long as that stays under the texture-size limit (4096 px when no other limit is set). If they can't be merged, the atlas is evicted and starts over. During idle callbacks it also pre-fills printable ASCII so the first screen of output is mostly cache hits.

Then the drawing. GlyphRenderer keeps a typed array with 11 floats (44 bytes) per cell: offset, size, texture page, texture coordinates, texture size and cell position. Each of those attributes advances once per instance. The whole visible grid then goes to the GPU in a single call:

gl.drawElementsInstanced(
  gl.TRIANGLE_STRIP, 4, gl.UNSIGNED_BYTE, 0,
  bufferLength / Constants.INDICES_PER_CELL
);

That is one unit quad with four vertices, drawn once per cell. The CPU's job per frame shrinks to filling a float array for the dirty rows; there are no DOM nodes to lay out and no discarded spans to collect. The fragment shader picks the right texture page from an array of samplers, up to 32 pages or the device's texture-unit limit, whichever is lower.

One detail matters for split panes. In CharAtlasCache, terminals whose font and color configuration match share one atlas: the cache finds an entry with an equal config and adds the new terminal to its ownedBy list. Five panes with the same theme rasterise a glyph once, not five times.

What WebGL does not fix

The xterm.js flow control guide puts the terminal's input throughput at "5 - 35 MB/s", against producers that can push "several GB/s." Most of that is parsing, and the parser is the same code under both renderers. write() buffers and returns at once, and the buffer has a hard limit: "Any data beyond that limit gets discarded." Five agents flooding at once still share that parsing time on one main thread. WebGL frees up the frame budget the DOM renderer was spending on layout, and that time goes back to parsing and to your input.

WebGL can also go away under you. The addon's README warns that browsers "may drop WebGL contexts for various reasons like OOM or after the system has been suspended," and exposes onContextLoss so the app can dispose the addon. When an app does that, it ends up back on the DOM renderer. VS Code's default, per its terminal appearance docs, is auto: try WebGL, "fall back to the DOM renderer" if that fails. The same page lists Linux VMs, browsers without WebGL and outdated drivers as places where WebGL may not work well.

In code, the defensive load looks like this:

import { WebglAddon } from '@xterm/addon-webgl';

function loadWebgl(term) {
  try {
    const webgl = new WebglAddon();
    webgl.onContextLoss(() => webgl.dispose());
    term.loadAddon(webgl);
    return true;
  } catch {
    return false; // stays on the DOM renderer
  }
}

If you have ever seen one pane in a terminal app suddenly feel slower after the laptop woke from sleep, a dropped context and a silent fallback is one candidate worth checking.

A benchmark you can run

Save this as bench.html, serve the folder (npx serve . works), and open it twice: once with ?r=dom and once with ?r=webgl. It writes about 200,000 colored log lines in 200 chunks, waits for each chunk's write callback, and records how often the page managed to paint while it was busy.

<!doctype html>
<link rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://unpkg.com/@xterm/xterm@6.0.0/css/xterm.css">
<div id="t" style="width:900px;height:500px"></div>
<pre id="out"></pre>
<script type="module">
import { Terminal } from 'https://esm.sh/@xterm/xterm@6.0.0';
import { WebglAddon }
  from 'https://esm.sh/@xterm/addon-webgl@0.19.0';

const q = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
const mode = q.get('r') ?? 'dom';
const term = new Terminal({ scrollback: 1000 });
term.open(document.getElementById('t'));
if (mode === 'webgl') term.loadAddon(new WebglAddon());

const line = (i) =>
  `\x1b[32m[agent]\x1b[0m step ${i} src/f${i % 97}.ts ` +
  `\x1b[33mok\x1b[0m ${'.'.repeat(i % 40)}\r\n`;
const chunks = [];
for (let c = 0; c < 200; c++) {
  let s = '';
  for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) s += line(c * 1000 + i);
  chunks.push(s);
}

let frames = 0, worst = 0, last = performance.now();
let running = true;
const tick = (now) => {
  frames++;
  worst = Math.max(worst, now - last);
  last = now;
  if (running) requestAnimationFrame(tick);
};
requestAnimationFrame(tick);

const t0 = performance.now();
for (const chunk of chunks) {
  await new Promise((done) => term.write(chunk, done));
}
running = false;
const ms = performance.now() - t0;
document.getElementById('out').textContent =
  `${mode}: ${ms.toFixed(0)} ms, ${frames} frames, ` +
  `worst gap ${worst.toFixed(1)} ms`;
</script>

Read the three numbers together. Total time is mostly parser time, so expect it to move less than you'd guess. Frame count and worst gap are the renderer's story: how often the page got to paint, and the longest stretch where it couldn't. A long worst gap is the keystroke that shows up late. To mimic five panes, duplicate the div and the terminal five times and write to all of them in the same loop.

I haven't run this across a range of machines, so I won't quote numbers. Run it on yours, and on the oldest laptop you can borrow. The write callback fires when the parser finishes a chunk, per the write API docs, not when pixels hit the screen, so the final frame lands a moment after the total.

Where Hermes IDE sits in this

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes runs each agent (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI and others) in its own real terminal, with split panes so sessions sit side by side. Those terminals are xterm.js: the package.json pins @xterm/xterm 6.0.0 and depends on @xterm/addon-webgl. The README describes the rendering as "GPU-accelerated (WebGL) where the system supports it," which is the same try-WebGL, keep-DOM-as-fallback idea VS Code uses.


Hermes 2.3.4: Codex and Claude Code in split panes, each in its own hermes/ worktree, with the sessions sidebar showing status, context use, cost and branch.

None of that is specific to Hermes. Any app built on xterm.js can load the same addon, and VS Code has done so by default since its 1.55 release. Hermes is free to download, source-available under BSL 1.1, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and is not affiliated with any agent vendor. Download it here, or read the code on GitHub.

If this was useful

The glyph atlas is a small system-design lesson hiding in a terminal: a cache keyed on exactly what makes an entry unique, an eviction plan for when it fills, batching a thousand updates into one unit of work per frame, and sharing one expensive resource across tenants with the same config. Those are the trade-offs interviewers want you to say out loud. The System Design Pocket Guide: Interviews walks through 15 real designs step by step, with that reasoning on every page.

articles.title: Your Agent's Tests Pass. Mutate Only Its Diff With Stryker and See If They Notice
articles.description: Green tests from an agent prove the tests run. Mutate only the files its branch changed with StrykerJS and read the survivors as untested lines.
articles.body_html:
• Book: AI Agents Pocket Guide
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Coverage on the agent's new file is 100% and both of its tests are green. It added a discount rule and wrote two tests for it. You are about to merge. The rule and its tests:

// src/discount.ts
export function discount(total: number): number {
  if (total >= 100) {
    return total * 0.1;
  }
  return 0;
}

// src/discount.test.ts
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { discount } from "./discount";

test("big orders get a discount", () => {
  expect(discount(150)).toBeGreaterThan(0);
});

test("small orders get none", () => {
  expect(discount(50)).toBe(0);
});

Every line runs. Every branch runs. Now change >= to >. Both tests still pass, because nothing checks an order of exactly 100. Change * to /. Still green: 1,500 is greater than 0 too. Two real bugs, zero red tests.

Coverage tells you a line executed. It does not tell you a test would fail if that line were wrong. Mutation testing measures the second thing, and you can point it at only the code the agent touched.

What a mutant is, and why "survived" is the useful word

A mutation tester makes small, deliberate changes to your source, one at a time, and runs your tests against each changed version. Each changed version is a mutant. StrykerJS is the best-known one for JavaScript and TypeScript. Its mutator list includes both edits above, and more: a >= b becomes a > b or a < b, arithmetic operators get swapped, if conditions get replaced with true or false, and whole blocks get emptied.

Stryker's definitions are blunt. A mutant is Killed when "at least one test failed while this mutant was active." It Survived when "all tests passed while this mutant was active, the mutant survived. You're missing a test for it." No coverage means no test even ran that code. The mutation score is detected mutants (killed plus timed out) divided by valid mutants.

So the survivors are a list of lines where a plausible bug would ship and your tests would stay green. That is a better review checklist than a coverage number, and it is the right question to ask about tests an agent wrote to make its own change pass.


Killed mutants get caught by a test. Survivors walk out the door.

This is a different check from diff coverage. diff-cover will "automatically find diff lines that need test coverage," which catches lines no test runs at all. The discount tests above would pass diff-cover with a perfect score. Mutation testing catches the lines that run but are never really asserted on.

Step 1: install Stryker with the Vitest runner

StrykerJS 10 is the current major (v10.1.1, October 23, 2026), and v10.0.0 dropped Node.js 20: you need Node 22 or newer. The getting-started guide runs an interactive setup with npm init stryker@latest. If you already know you use Vitest, install the pieces directly:

npm i -D @stryker-mutator/core \
  @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner

Then a small stryker.config.json at the repo root:

{
  "testRunner": "vitest",
  "reporters": ["clear-text", "progress", "html", "json"],
  "thresholds": { "high": 80, "low": 60, "break": 60 }
}

A few things from the configuration reference matter here. The json reporter writes reports/mutation/mutation.json, which you will read in step 3. The html reporter writes reports/mutation.html. With break set, Stryker exits with code 1 when the score falls below it, so a script or CI job can fail on it. The Vitest runner always uses per-test coverage analysis, so each mutant only runs the tests that cover it, and it does not support Vitest browser mode.

Leave mutate out of the config. The script in step 2 supplies it.

Step 2: mutate only the files the agent's branch changed

The agent's work lives on its own branch. Three-dot diff gives you what that branch changed since it split from main. The git docs put it this way: git diff A...B "is equivalent to git diff $(git merge-base A B) B," so commits that landed on main in the meantime don't leak in.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/mutate-diff.sh: mutate only this branch's changes
set -euo pipefail
base="${1:-main}"

files=$(git diff --name-only --diff-filter=d \
  "$base"...HEAD -- 'src/*.ts' \
  ':!*.test.ts' ':!*.spec.ts' | paste -sd, -)

if [ -z "$files" ]; then
  echo "No changed source files since $base."
  exit 0
fi

npx stryker run --mutate "$files"

Why each piece is there:

  • --diff-filter=d drops deleted files. In git, a lowercase filter letter excludes that status, so there is no point asking Stryker to mutate a file that no longer exists.
  • The :! pathspecs drop test files. This matters because a --mutate value on the command line "will completely replace" the one in the config, per the Stryker docs, so Stryker's default of skipping test files no longer applies.
  • paste -sd, - joins the paths with commas, which is the list form --mutate takes.

Three-dot diff compares commits, so it misses edits the agent hasn't committed yet. If you want those too, diff the merge base against the working tree instead: git diff --name-only $(git merge-base main HEAD). New untracked files still won't show up until they are added.

If a branch touches one function in a 600-line file, you can go narrower. mutate accepts line ranges like src/app.js:1-11, so you can turn the hunks of git diff -U0 into ranges if a file-level run is too slow. File level is a good default anyway: survivors in the untouched code around the change tell you how much the agent's edit leans on code nobody really tests.

For repeat runs while the agent iterates, add --incremental. Stryker stores results in reports/stryker-incremental.json and reuses them on the next run, so only mutants affected by new edits get tested again.

Step 3: turn survivors into a list someone can act on

The HTML report is good for browsing. For handing work back to an agent, you want plain lines. The JSON report follows the mutation-testing report schema: files is keyed by path, and each mutant has a mutatorName, a location with a 1-based start.line, an optional replacement, and a status.

# scripts/survivors.jq
.files
| to_entries[]
| .key as $file
| .value.mutants[]
| select(.status == "Survived"
    or .status == "NoCoverage")
| "\($file):\(.location.start.line)"
  + "  \(.mutatorName)"
  + "  -> \(.replacement // "")"

jq -r -f scripts/survivors.jq \
  reports/mutation/mutation.json

Each line names a file, a line number, the kind of mutation, and the code that replaced the original. For the discount example, working it through by hand, you'd expect two survivors, on the if line and the return line inside it: the >= boundary and the * to / swap. The negated comparison, the true/false conditions and the emptied block all break one of the two tests, so those get killed.

Each survivor tells you which assertion is missing. A test at exactly 100 kills the boundary mutant. Asserting the actual amount instead of "greater than zero" kills the arithmetic one:

test("discount starts at exactly 100", () => {
  expect(discount(100)).toBeCloseTo(10);
  expect(discount(99)).toBe(0);
});

test("discount is ten percent", () => {
  expect(discount(150)).toBeCloseTo(15);
});

toBeCloseTo is there because multiplying by 0.1 isn't always exact in floating point (3 * 0.1 is 0.30000000000000004), and the rate may change later.

Not every survivor is a missing test. Some mutants are equivalent: the change produces code that behaves the same, and no test could kill it. Logging lines and defensive defaults often land here. Read the list as review questions, not as a to-do list the agent must clear to zero.

Step 4: run it in the agent's worktree, before you land

This part is where Hermes IDE fits, and I build Hermes, so weigh it with that in mind. In Hermes, ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux) starts each task on its own hermes/<name> branch in its own git worktree. That is exactly the setup mutate-diff.sh wants: the branch has only the agent's changes, and running Stryker there doesn't touch your main checkout or another agent's folder.


The Review Desk's Worktrees tab: one Hermes worktree each for orders-api, web-app and orders-types under ~/code, with each worktree's hermes/ branch, task, age and disk size.

Open a plain terminal in the task's worktree and run the two scripts. If you want the run to happen every time, Hermes reads a done_when list from .hermes/worktree.toml as the task's default checks (recipe docs), so your own checks decide when a task counts as done:

# .hermes/worktree.toml
setup = ["npm ci"]
done_when = ["npm test", "bash scripts/mutate-diff.sh"]

Think about cost before you do that. Even with only the diff mutated and per-test coverage, a mutation run executes tests many times. On a big change it can take minutes. Running it by hand before Land is a reasonable middle ground.

Then hand the survivors back. The Review Desk (⌘G, Ctrl+Shift+G on Windows and Linux) shows the task's changes by turn or by file, and a line comment there goes back to the agent that wrote the line. Put a comment on the if line of discount.ts saying "a mutant changing >= to > survives; add a test at exactly 100," and the agent gets a concrete, checkable job instead of "write better tests." The other route is pasting the survivors.jq output into the agent's terminal as its next prompt.


The Review Desk (⌘G) in By turn view for a Claude Code task in orders-api: two turns listed, turn 1's diff of src/db.ts, the changed-files list, and a commit message drafted from the turns.

When the rerun comes back with the survivors you agreed to fix gone, Land commits, opens a pull request or merges locally into the branch the task started from, and it can be undone.

None of steps 1 to 3 needs Hermes. git worktree add -b agent/discount ../discount gives you the same isolated branch, and the scripts run the same way there.

What this does and doesn't tell you

A high mutation score on the diff says the agent's tests react when its code changes in the ways Stryker knows how to change it. It does not say the code does what the ticket asked. A test suite can kill every mutant and still encode the wrong business rule, so you still read the diff.

It also doesn't replace property-based tests, which search for inputs that break an invariant. Mutation testing grades the tests you have. Property tests generate new ones: use them to find inputs you didn't think of, and Stryker to check the assertions on the ones you did.

What it does give you, cheaply, is a way to stop taking "all tests pass" at face value when the same agent wrote the code and the tests.

If this was useful

Agents grading their own work is one of the core guardrail problems: the check has to come from outside the loop that produced the change. My AI Agents Pocket Guide covers that and the other patterns for keeping autonomous agents honest, in a short read.

If you want each agent's work on its own branch with a review step before it lands, Hermes IDE is source-available under BSL 1.1 and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. It is on GitHub if you want to look under the hood.
